items.title: Rise of the INC & the Moderate Phase (1885-1905)
items.body:
### Rise of the INC and the Moderates

**In one line**
The Indian National Congress (INC) began in 1885 as a polite, loyal body of educated Indians who asked the British for reforms through letters and speeches rather than protest.

**Why it is asked**
This is where organised Indian nationalism starts, so the exam loves the founding facts (year, place, people, number of delegates) and the difference between the early Moderates and the later Extremists.

**The story**
Before the Congress, discontent was voiced by small regional groups of landlords and professionals: the **Landholders' Society (1837)**, the **British Indian Association (1851)**, the **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870)**, the **Indian National Association (S.N. Banerjee, 1876)** and the **Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884)**. Several of them later merged into the Congress. The INC itself was founded in **December 1885** at the **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay**, organised by the retired British official **A.O. Hume**, with **W.C. Bonnerjee** as first president and **72 delegates**. The **Safety Valve theory** says Hume wanted the Congress to let Indian anger escape peacefully, like steam from a valve, so it would not explode into revolt. For its first twenty years the Congress was led by **Moderates** — **Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta** — who trusted British fair play. Their method was **constitutional agitation** (petitions, resolutions, speeches), mocked by later leaders as *political mendicancy* (begging). Their demands stopped at **self-government within the Empire**, never full independence: Indianisation of the services, less military spending, more Indians on the councils, and civil rights. Naoroji's lasting contribution was the **Drain of Wealth theory** in his book *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901), which argued that Britain was steadily draining India's wealth away.

**Pre-Congress associations — who founded what**

| Association | Year | Founder(s) |
|---|---|---|
| British Indian Association (Calcutta) | 1851 | Radhakant Deb (president) / Debendranath Tagore |
| Poona Sarvajanik Sabha | 1870 | M.G. Ranade & others |
| Indian National Association (Calcutta) | 1876 | Surendranath Banerjee & Ananda Mohan Bose |
| Madras Mahajan Sabha | 1884 | M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer, P. Ananda Charlu |

**Don't confuse** Ranade = Poona (west); Banerjee = Calcutta (east); Veeraraghavachariar and Subramania Iyer = Madras (south).

**What the Moderates won** They believed in constitutional agitation through petitions, meetings and resolutions; their demands included Indianisation of the civil services and reduction of military expenditure. Their one tangible achievement is usually said to be the **Indian Councils Act of 1892**, which enlarged the councils and let members discuss the budget.

**Picture it**

| 'First' | Person | Session |
|---|---|---|
| First president | W.C. Bonnerjee | 1885 |
| First Muslim president | Badruddin Tyabji | 1887 |
| First woman president | Annie Besant | 1917 |
| First Indian woman president | Sarojini Naidu | 1925 |

**Terms explained**
- **Moderates** — early Congress leaders who sought gradual reform through legal, constitutional means.
- **Political mendicancy** — a critic's term meaning 'begging politics', because the Moderates only petitioned.
- **Drain of Wealth** — the idea that British rule transferred India's resources to Britain without return.
- **Safety Valve theory** — the view that the Congress was meant to release discontent harmlessly.

**Don't confuse**
- **A.O. Hume (organiser)** with **W.C. Bonnerjee (first president)** — Hume set it up, Bonnerjee chaired the first session.
- **First woman president Annie Besant (1917)** with **first Indian woman president Sarojini Naidu (1925)** — Besant was Irish-British.

**Remember it**
Moderate quartet **'NGBM' = Naoroji, Gokhale, Banerjee, Mehta** — they wrote letters, they did not march.

**TL;DR**
- INC founded December 1885 at Bombay by A.O. Hume; first president W.C. Bonnerjee; 72 delegates.
- Moderates (1885-1905) used petitions and resolutions, seeking self-rule within the Empire, not freedom.
- Naoroji's Drain of Wealth theory (1901) gave nationalism its economic argument.
- Firsts: Tyabji (Muslim, 1887), Besant (woman, 1917), Naidu (Indian woman, 1925).

items.title: Extremist Phase, Swadeshi & Revolutionaries (1905-1917)
items.body:
### Extremists, Swadeshi and the Revolutionaries

**In one line**
From 1905 a bolder generation stopped petitioning and started boycotting British goods, demanding Swaraj (self-rule), and a few turned to armed revolt.

**Why it is asked**
The Partition of Bengal, the Swadeshi Movement, the Surat Split and the early revolutionaries are among the most frequently tested facts in modern history, and the exam often mixes up their leaders and dates.

**The story**
The trigger was **Lord Curzon's Partition of Bengal (1905)**, which split Bengal into a Muslim-majority east and a Hindu-majority west — widely seen as 'divide and rule'. The outrage launched the **Swadeshi and Boycott Movement**: Indians boycotted British cloth and goods and promoted khadi, indigenous industry and national schools. **Rabindranath Tagore** opposed the partition and popularised **Raksha Bandhan** (tying threads on one another) as a symbol of Hindu–Muslim unity. The partition was finally **annulled in 1911**. This mood lifted the **Extremists** — the **Lal-Bal-Pal** trio (**Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal**) and **Aurobindo Ghose** — who wanted mass action, not polite requests. Tilak's cry *'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'* captured the new spirit; he also wrote *Gita Rahasya* and used Ganpati and Shivaji festivals to spread nationalism. The clash of methods broke the Congress open at the **Surat Split (1907)**; the two wings reunited only at **Lucknow (1916)**. Alongside this public politics ran **revolutionary nationalism**: Bengal's secret societies **Anushilan Samiti** and **Jugantar**, Aurobindo's paper **Bande Mataram** and the **Alipore Bomb Case (1908-09)**, and the hanging of young **Khudiram Bose (1908)**. Overseas, the **Ghadar Party (1913, USA)**, founded by Indian immigrants there,, founded by Indian immigrants there, — **Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, Rashbehari Bose** — planned an armed revolt during the First World War. Later the **HSRA — Hindustan Socialist Republican Association** (Bhagat Singh, Chandrasekhar Azad, Sukhdev, Rajguru) carried the torch, with Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru executed in **1931**; the **Karachi Congress session (1931)** condemned these executions. On the constitutional side, the **Muslim League was founded (1906, Dhaka)**, the **Morley-Minto Reforms (1909)** introduced **separate electorates** for Muslims (but no responsible government) and saw **Satyendra Prasanna Sinha** become the first Indian on the Viceroy's Executive Council, and the **Home Rule Movement (1916)** was run by Tilak (Maharashtra) and Annie Besant (Madras).

**Picture it**

```
1905 Partition of Bengal → Swadeshi/Boycott → Extremists rise
   1906 Muslim League      1907 Surat Split
   1909 Morley-Minto        1911 Partition annulled
   1913 Ghadar Party        1916 Home Rule + Lucknow reunion
```

**Terms explained**
- **Swaraj** — self-rule; for Extremists it meant real self-government, not reforms.
- **Swadeshi** — 'of one's own country': using Indian-made goods and shunning British ones.
- **Boycott** — refusing to buy British goods or use British institutions as a protest.
- **Separate electorates** — a system where Muslims voted only for Muslim candidates, kept apart from others.
- **Revolutionary nationalism** — the belief that British rule could be ended only by armed action.

**Don't confuse**
- **Moderates (petitions)** with **Extremists (boycott, Swaraj)** — same party, opposite methods.
- **Partition of Bengal (1905, Curzon)** with its **annulment (1911)** — do not merge the two dates.
- **Ghadar Party (USA, diaspora)** with the **Muslim League (Dhaka, communal politics)**.

**Remember it**
**'Lal-Bal-Pal' = Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, (Bipin Chandra) Pal** — the three extremist voices.

**TL;DR**
- Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 (annulled 1911), triggering the Swadeshi/Boycott Movement.
- Lal-Bal-Pal led the Extremists; Tilak coined 'Swaraj is my birthright'.
- Surat Split (1907) divided Congress; reunion at Lucknow (1916).
- Revolutionaries: Anushilan/Jugantar, Alipore Bomb Case (1908-09), Ghadar Party (1913), HSRA.
- Muslim League (1906, Dhaka); Morley-Minto (1909) brought separate electorates.

items.title: Mass Movements: 1919-1934
items.body:
### Mass movements under Gandhi (1919-1934)

**In one line**
After 1919 the freedom struggle became a mass movement of millions, as Gandhi turned Congress protest into nationwide non-violent campaigns.

**Why it is asked**
This decade carries the most famous events — Jallianwala Bagh, Non-Cooperation, the Dandi March — and the exam tests their causes, dates and why Gandhi started or stopped each one.

**The story**
The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** let the government jail Indians without trial, provoking protests. At **Amritsar** on **13 April 1919**, troops under **General Dyer** opened fire on a peaceful gathering — the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** (official toll about 379 dead) — and **Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood** in protest. The anger fed Gandhi's **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)**, which merged with the **Khilafat Movement** (the Ali Brothers) to unite Hindus and Muslims; Indians boycotted schools, courts, titles and foreign goods. Gandhi abruptly **withdrew it after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922)**, where a mob burnt a police station, because violence broke his non-violence rule. When the movement paused, **C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party (1923)** to enter the legislative councils and obstruct the government from within. Next came the **Simon Commission (1927)**, an all-British body met with 'Simon, go back', during whose protest **Lala Lajpat Rai was fatally injured**. The Congress replied with the **Nehru Report (1928)** under Motilal Nehru, demanding Dominion Status. Finally the **Civil Disobedience Movement (1930)** opened with the **Dandi Salt March**; it was paused by the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)**, discussed at the **Round Table Conferences (1930-32)**, and complicated by the **Communal Award (1932)** and the **Poona Pact (1932)**.

**Picture it**

| Event | Year |
|---|---|
| Rowlatt Act / Jallianwala Bagh | 1919 |
| Non-Cooperation / Khilafat | 1920-22 |
| Chauri Chaura | 1922 |
| Dandi March / CDM | 1930 |
| Gandhi-Irwin Pact | 1931 |
| GoI Act | 1935 |

**Terms explained**
- **Non-Cooperation** — refusing to cooperate with the government by boycotting its schools, courts, titles and goods.
- **Khilafat Movement** — a Muslim campaign to protect the Ottoman Caliph, which Gandhi joined to build Hindu-Muslim unity.
- **Civil Disobedience** — deliberately but peacefully breaking unjust laws, like making salt against the salt law.
- **Dominion Status** — self-government within the British Empire, like Canada, short of full independence.

**Don't confuse**
- **Non-Cooperation (1920-22)** with **Civil Disobedience (1930)** — the first boycotted institutions, the second broke laws.
- **Chauri Chaura (ended NCM, 1922)** with **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (paused CDM, 1931)**.
- **Simon Commission (1927, British body)** with the **Nehru Report (1928, Indian reply)**.

**Remember it**
Gandhi starts a movement on a principle and stops it on a principle — Chauri Chaura's violence is why he called off Non-Cooperation.

**TL;DR**
- Rowlatt Act (1919) allowed detention without trial; Jallianwala Bagh massacre 13 April 1919 under General Dyer.
- Non-Cooperation (1920-22) merged with the Khilafat Movement; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922).
- Swaraj Party (1923) founded by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru for council entry.
- Simon Commission (1927) was all-British; Lajpat Rai fatally injured; Nehru Report (1928) demanded Dominion Status.
- Civil Disobedience began with the Dandi March (1930); Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931.

Non-Cooperation (1920-22) merged with the Khilafat Movement; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922).
Swaraj Party (1923) founded by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru for council entry.
Simon Commission (1927) was all-British; met with 'Simon, go back'; Lajpat Rai fatally injured.
Nehru Report (1928), chaired by Motilal Nehru, demanded Dominion Status.

items.title: From Purna Swaraj to Independence (1929-1947)
items.body:
### From Purna Swaraj to Independence

**In one line**
From 1929 the Congress openly demanded complete independence, and after the Quit India struggle and a chain of failed British missions, India became free (and partitioned) in 1947.

**Why it is asked**
The final push to freedom — Purna Swaraj, the 1935 Act, Quit India and the missions of 1940-47 — is heavily tested, often as a chronology or a 'which mission did what' match.

**The story**
At the **Lahore Session (1929)**, president **Jawaharlal Nehru**, the Congress adopted the **Purna Swaraj** (complete independence) resolution and fixed **26 January 1930** as the first Independence Day. The **Government of India Act, 1935** then gave **provincial autonomy** and planned a federation; the Congress won the **1937 provincial elections** and formed ministries, which **resigned in 1939** when Britain dragged India into the Second World War without consent. In August 1942, with the war going badly, Gandhi launched the **Quit India Movement** at Bombay on **8 August 1942** with the call **'Do or Die'**. The British jailed the top leaders at once, so the movement was carried underground by **Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia and Sucheta Kripalani**. The last years saw a run of British offers and plans — the **August Offer (1940)**, the **Cripps Mission (1942)**, the **Cabinet Mission (1946)**, **Direct Action Day (1946)**, the **RIN Mutiny (1946)** and finally the **Mountbatten Plan (1947)** — ending with the **Indian Independence Act (1947)** that created India and Pakistan.

**Picture it**

| Step | Year | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| August Offer | 1940 | Dominion status offer; rejected |
| Cripps Mission | 1942 | Post-war Dominion status; rejected |
| Cabinet Mission | 1946 | Federal union, province grouping |
| Direct Action Day | 1946 | League's call; Calcutta riots |
| RIN Mutiny | 1946 | Naval ratings' revolt, Bombay |
| Mountbatten Plan | 1947 | Partition; freedom by 15 Aug 1947 |
| Indian Independence Act | 1947 | Created India and Pakistan |

**Terms explained**
- **Purna Swaraj** — complete independence, as opposed to Dominion Status within the Empire.
- **Provincial autonomy** — provinces running their own affairs with elected Indian ministries (from the 1935 Act).
- **Quit India** — the 1942 demand that the British leave India immediately.
- **RIN Mutiny** — the Royal Indian Navy ratings' revolt at Bombay in 1946.

**Don't confuse**
- **Cripps Mission (1942, post-war Dominion status)** with the **Cabinet Mission (1946, federal union)**.
- **Mountbatten Plan (the partition plan)** with the **Indian Independence Act (the law that enacted it)**.
- **Purna Swaraj (1929 goal)** with **Dominion Status (the Nehru Report / Cripps ceiling)**.

**Remember it**
Road to 1947 in order — **'August-Cripps-Cabinet-Mountbatten'** are the four big offers/plans.

**TL;DR**
- Lahore Session (1929, Nehru) adopted Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was the first Independence Day.
- GoI Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy; Congress won 1937 elections, resigned ministries in 1939.
- Quit India launched 8 August 1942 with 'Do or Die'; underground leaders included Aruna Asaf Ali and JP Narayan.
- Cripps (1942) and Cabinet Mission (1946) both failed; Mountbatten Plan (1947) recommended Partition.
- The Indian Independence Act (1947) created India and Pakistan.
keyPoints: Lahore Session (1929, Nehru) adopted Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 was the first Independence Day.
GoI Act 1935 gave provincial autonomy; Congress won 1937 elections and formed ministries, resigning in 1939.
Quit India launched 8 August 1942 with 'Do or Die'; underground leaders included Aruna Asaf Ali and JP Narayan.
Cripps Mission (1942) and Cabinet Mission (1946) both failed to prevent partition.
Direct Action Day (1946) led to Calcutta riots; the RIN Mutiny (1946) shook the Raj.
Mountbatten Plan (1947) recommended Partition; the Indian Independence Act (July 1947) created India and Pakistan.

items.title: Subhas Chandra Bose, the Forward Bloc & the INA
items.body:
### Subhas Chandra Bose and the INA

**In one line**
Subhas Chandra Bose broke from Gandhi's non-violence and built an army abroad — the Indian National Army — to win freedom by force.

**Why it is asked**
Bose's two Congress presidencies, his resignation, the Forward Bloc and the INA Trials are standard exam facts, and his slogans are favourite one-liners.

**The story**
**Subhas Chandra Bose** was elected **Congress President at Haripura (1938)** and again at **Tripuri (1939)**, but **resigned in 1939** after clashing with the Working Committee and Gandhi over methods. He then founded the **Forward Bloc (1939)** to unite the radical left within the Congress. Escaping British India, he reached Germany and then Japan, where he **reorganised the Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj)** from Indian prisoners of war, including the **Rani of Jhansi women's regiment**. His stirring calls were **'Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom'** and **'Jai Hind'**. The INA fought alongside Japan in north-east India. Although it was defeated militarily, the **INA Trials (1945-46)** of its officers at the **Red Fort** in Delhi roused enormous public sympathy and put the British under pressure, helping convince them that even Indian soldiers could no longer be trusted to hold the Raj together.

**Picture it**

| Milestone | Year |
|---|---|
| Congress President, Haripura | 1938 |
| Congress President, Tripuri; resigned | 1939 |
| Forward Bloc founded | 1939 |
| INA reorganised (with Japanese support) | 1943 |
| INA Trials at Red Fort | 1945-46 |

**Terms explained**
- **Forward Bloc** — the left-wing group Bose founded inside the Congress in 1939.
- **Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj)** — the army of Indians, mostly ex-POWs, that fought the British with Japanese help.
- **Rani of Jhansi regiment** — the women's unit of the INA.
- **INA Trials** — the 1945-46 court cases against INA officers at the Red Fort.

**Don't confuse**
- **Haripura (1938)** with **Tripuri (1939)** — his first and second presidencies; he resigned after Tripuri.
- **Forward Bloc (party, 1939)** with the **INA (army, 1943 reorganisation)**.

**Remember it**
Bose = 'blood for freedom' — the leader who chose an army over a petition.

**TL;DR**
- Bose was Congress President at Haripura (1938) and Tripuri (1939); resigned in 1939.
- He founded the Forward Bloc (1939) to rally the Congress left.
- He reorganised the INA (Azad Hind Fauj) with Japanese support, including the Rani of Jhansi regiment.
- Slogans: 'Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom' and 'Jai Hind'.
- The INA Trials (1945-46) at the Red Fort generated mass nationalist sentiment.

items.title: Peasant & Tribal Movements (with AP angle)
items.body:
### Peasant and tribal movements

**In one line**
Beside the Congress, peasants and tribal communities rose repeatedly against rents, moneylenders and colonial forest laws, adding a grassroots layer to the freedom struggle.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests the match of movement to leader and region, and APPSC in particular asks the Andhra tribal revolts, especially Alluri Sitarama Raju.

**The story**
Peasant anger ran through the whole colonial period. The **Indigo Revolt (1859-60)** in Bengal, which inspired the play *Neel Darpan*, protested forced indigo cultivation; the **Deccan Riots (1875)** targeted moneylenders (*sahukars*) and led to the Relief Act of 1879; the **Pabna Movement (1873-85)** formed an agrarian league against oppressive rents. In the Gandhian era, **Vallabhbhai Patel** led the **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)** against a steep tax rise and earned the title *'Sardar'*. The **All India Kisan Sabha (1936)** under **Swami Sahajanand Saraswati** demanded the end of zamindari, and the **Tebhaga (1946)** and **Telangana (1946-52)** struggles pushed for a bigger share for sharecroppers and against the Nizam's jagirdars. Tribal communities also revolted: the **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56)** under **Sidhu and Kanhu** in the **Rajmahal Hills**, the **Kol Mutiny (1831)**, and the **Munda Ulgulan (Birsa Munda, 1899-1900)** in **Chhotanagpur**. In **Andhra**, the **Koya Revolts** (Godavari), the **Khond Uprisings** (Srikakulam/Visakhapatnam, under Chakra Bisoi) and above all **Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion (1922-24)** resisted colonial forest laws.

**Picture it**

| Movement | Region | Leader/Note |
|---|---|---|
| Indigo Revolt (1859-60) | Bengal | Biswas brothers; *Neel Darpan* |
| Deccan Riots (1875) | Maharashtra | against sahukars; Relief Act 1879 |
| Pabna Movement (1873-85) | Bengal | Ishan Chandra Roy; agrarian league |
| Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) | Gujarat | Vallabhbhai Patel ('Sardar') |
| All India Kisan Sabha (1936) | national | Swami Sahajanand Saraswati |
| Tebhaga (1946) | Bengal | sharecroppers; two-thirds share |
| Telangana (1946-52) | Andhra/Telangana | against Nizam's jagirdars; CPI-led |

**Terms explained**
- **Satyagraha** — Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance; at Bardoli, a no-tax campaign.
- **Sahukar** — a village moneylender, the target of the Deccan Riots.
- **Zamindari** — the landlord-based land system the Kisan Sabha wanted abolished.
- **Ulgulan** — the Mundari word for 'great tumult', the name of Birsa Munda's uprising.
- **Tebhaga** — the demand that sharecroppers keep two-thirds (not half) of the crop.

**Don't confuse**
- **Santhal Rebellion (Sidhu & Kanhu)** with the **Munda Ulgulan (Birsa Munda)** — different tribes and leaders.
- **Bardoli Satyagraha (Patel, no-tax)** with the **All India Kisan Sabha (Sahajanand, anti-zamindari)**.
- **Alluri's Rampa Rebellion (Andhra tribal)** with the Congress-led mass movements.

**Remember it**
In Andhra, one name links tribe and freedom struggle — **Alluri Sitarama Raju, the 'Manyam Veerudu' of the Rampa Rebellion (1922-24)**.

**TL;DR**
- Indigo Revolt (1859-60) inspired Neel Darpan; Deccan Riots (1875) led to the 1879 Relief Act.
- Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) made Patel 'Sardar'; All India Kisan Sabha (1936) under Sahajanand sought zamindari abolition.
- Santhal Rebellion (Sidhu & Kanhu, 1855-56); Munda Ulgulan (Birsa Munda, 1899-1900).
- Andhra: Koya and Khond revolts, and Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) against forest laws.
keyPoints: Indigo Revolt (1859-60, Bengal) inspired the play Neel Darpan; Deccan Riots (1875) led to the 1879 Relief Act.
Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) under Vallabhbhai Patel earned him the title 'Sardar'.
All India Kisan Sabha (1936) founded by Swami Sahajanand Saraswati demanded abolition of zamindari.
Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) led by Sidhu and Kanhu; Munda Ulgulan led by Birsa Munda.
In Andhra, the Koya and Khond revolts and Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) resisted colonial forest laws.
Non-Congress political currents: Muslim League, Communist Party of India, and the Justice/Liberal parties.

items.title: Key INC Sessions at a Glance
items.body:
### Key INC sessions

**In one line**
Many turning points of the freedom struggle were decided at particular Congress sessions, so the year-place-president-landmark set is worth memorising.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC and UPSC regularly ask 'which session adopted X' or 'who presided at Y', and the national songs' first singing is a recurring one-liner.

**The story**
The Congress met once a year, and each session is remembered for one decision. **Calcutta (1906)** under **Dadabhai Naoroji** saw the first official mention of **'Swaraj'**. The **Surat Split** came at **Surat (1907)** under **Rash Behari Ghosh**. **Lucknow (1916)** under **A.C. Mazumdar** brought the Lucknow Pact and the Moderate-Extremist reunion. **Nagpur (1920)** under **C. Vijayaraghavachariar** ratified Non-Cooperation and set up the Congress Working Committee. **Belgaum (1924)** was the only session **Gandhi** himself presided over. **Lahore (1929)** under **Jawaharlal Nehru** passed the Purna Swaraj resolution. **Karachi (1931)** under **Vallabhbhai Patel** adopted the Fundamental Rights resolution and condemned Bhagat Singh's execution. **Haripura (1938)** and **Tripuri (1939)** were **Subhas Chandra Bose's** two presidencies.

**Picture it**

| Year | Place | President | Landmark |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1885 | Bombay | W.C. Bonnerjee | First session; 72 delegates |
| 1906 | Calcutta | Dadabhai Naoroji | First mention of 'Swaraj' |
| 1907 | Surat | Rash Behari Ghosh | Surat Split |
| 1916 | Lucknow | A.C. Mazumdar | Lucknow Pact; Moderate-Extremist reunion |
| 1920 | Nagpur | C. Vijayaraghavachariar | Ratified Non-Cooperation; CWC set up |
| 1924 | Belgaum | M.K. Gandhi | Only session Gandhi presided |
| 1929 | Lahore | Jawaharlal Nehru | Purna Swaraj resolution |
| 1931 | Karachi | Vallabhbhai Patel | Fundamental Rights; condemned Bhagat Singh's execution |
| 1938 | Haripura | Subhas Chandra Bose | National Planning Committee |
| 1939 | Tripuri | Subhas Chandra Bose | Bose resigned; Forward Bloc |

**Terms explained**
- **Session** — the yearly meeting of the Congress, each with an elected president.
- **Congress Working Committee (CWC)** — the small executive body set up at Nagpur (1920) to run the party.
- **Fundamental Rights resolution** — the Karachi (1931) statement listing basic rights and economic goals.

**Don't confuse**
- **'Vande Mataram' (first sung Calcutta 1896)** with **'Jana Gana Mana' (first sung Calcutta 1911)** — both at Calcutta, fifteen years apart.
- **Lahore (1929, Purna Swaraj)** with **Karachi (1931, Fundamental Rights)**.

**Remember it**
Tie each session to its one headline: Nagpur = Non-Cooperation, Lahore = Purna Swaraj, Karachi = Fundamental Rights.

**TL;DR**
- Calcutta 1906 (Naoroji) first mentioned 'Swaraj'.
- Nagpur 1920 ratified Non-Cooperation and set up the CWC.
- Belgaum 1924 was the only session Gandhi presided over.
- Karachi 1931 (Patel) adopted Fundamental Rights and condemned Bhagat Singh's execution.
- 'Vande Mataram' first sung at Calcutta (1896); 'Jana Gana Mana' first sung at Calcutta (1911).

items.body:
### Swadeshi institutions, Surat Split and Ghadar (exam-focused)

**In one line**
These four facts — how Swadeshi built national schools, why Surat split the Congress, what the Ghadar Party was, and what the Lucknow Pact did — are repeat examination favourites.

**Why it is asked**
Each has appeared as a UPSC/APPSC question, so getting the exact wording right (first adoption, the real reason for the split, the Ghadar headquarters) directly earns marks.

**The story**
'Swadeshi' and 'Boycott' were **first adopted during the anti-Partition of Bengal agitation (1905)** — a key 'when was it first used' fact. The Swadeshi Movement did two things: it **revived indigenous crafts and industries** (khadi, Indian soap, matches, textiles) and it led to a revival of indigenous crafts and industries, and it led to a revival of indigenous crafts and industries, and it built **national education** — the **National Council of Education (NCE) was set up in 1906** and founded the **Bengal National College**, with **Aurobindo Ghose as its first principal**. The **Surat session of the Congress (1907)** ended in an open split. The Moderates and Extremists differed sharply over **methods** (petitions versus boycott), over the **goal of Swaraj**, and over the **presidential choice** (Rash Behari Ghosh). The **Surat Split** happened mainly because the **Extremists lost faith in the Moderates' capacity to negotiate** meaningful reform through petitions; quarrels over the presidency and over passing Swadeshi/boycott resolutions triggered the break, and the two wings **reunited at Lucknow (1916)**. The **Ghadar Party (1913)** was a **revolutionary association of Indians (mainly Punjabi emigrants) with its headquarters at San Francisco, USA**, led by **Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna and Kartar Singh Sarabha**, with **Rash Behari Bose** closely associated; it planned an armed revolt during the First World War (the failed Ghadar conspiracy of 1915). The **Lucknow Pact (1916)** was a Congress-Muslim League agreement (Tilak and Jinnah) in which the Congress **accepted separate electorates** in exchange for a joint demand for self-government.

**Picture it**

```
1905 Swadeshi/Boycott (anti-Partition) → 1906 NCE / Bengal National College
   → 1907 Surat Split → 1913 Ghadar (San Francisco) → 1916 Lucknow reunion + Pact
```

**Terms explained**
- **National Council of Education (NCE)** — a 1906 body that set up Indian-run colleges and schools during Swadeshi.
- **Separate electorates** — Muslims voting only for Muslim seats, which the Lucknow Pact accepted.
- **Ghadar** — the Urdu/Punjabi word for 'revolt' or 'mutiny'.
- **Ghadar conspiracy (1915)** — the party's planned wartime uprising, which was detected and crushed.

**Don't confuse**
- **National Council of Education (1906)** with the **Home Rule Leagues (1916)** — different decades, different aims.
- **Ghadar Party HQ = San Francisco** — not London, not Dhaka.
- The real cause of the **Surat Split** = Extremists' loss of faith in Moderate negotiation, not a personal quarrel alone.

**Remember it**
**Swadeshi 1905 builds NCE 1906 → Surat splits 1907 → Lucknow reunites 1916.**

**TL;DR**
- Swadeshi/Boycott were first adopted in the 1905 anti-Partition of Bengal agitation.
- Swadeshi revived indigenous crafts AND set up the National Council of Education (1906) / Bengal National College (Aurobindo first principal).
- Surat Split (1907): Extremists lost faith in the Moderates' capacity to negotiate; reunion at Lucknow (1916).
- Ghadar Party (1913): revolutionary Indians, HQ San Francisco; Har Dayal, Bhakna, Sarabha, Rash Behari Bose.
- Lucknow Pact (1916): Congress-League unity; Congress accepted separate electorates (Tilak-Jinnah).

The Swadeshi Movement revived indigenous crafts AND set up the National Council of Education (1906) / Bengal National College (Aurobindo first principal).
Surat Split (1907): Extremists lost faith in the Moderates' capacity to negotiate; reunion at Lucknow (1916).
Ghadar Party (1913) — revolutionary Indians with HQ at San Francisco; Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, Kartar Singh Sarabha, Rash Behari Bose.
Lucknow Pact (1916): Congress-League unity, Congress accepted separate electorates (Tilak-Jinnah).

items.title: Before the Congress: Associations and the Lytton–Ripon Years
items.body:
### Before the Congress: Associations and the Lytton–Ripon Years

**In one line**
Before 1885 educated Indians formed regional associations in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras; Lytton's harsh measures and the Ilbert Bill row then pushed them toward one all-India body.

**The story**
The three Presidency towns were the cradles of politics. In Calcutta the **Landholders' Society** (1837) and the **British Indian Association** (1851) spoke for zamindars; the **Indian Association** (1876) of **Surendranath Banerjee** spoke for the middle class. In Bombay came the **East India Association** (Naoroji, London 1866), the **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha** (1870) and the **Bombay Presidency Association** (1885). In Madras the Telugu merchant **Gajula Lakshminarasu Chetty** founded the **Madras Native Association** (1852) and later the **Madras Mahajan Sabha** (1884) appeared. Lord **Lytton** (1876–80) angered all of them — the **Vernacular Press Act**, the **Arms Act**, the ICS age cut and a lavish Durbar during famine. Under **Ripon** the **Ilbert Bill** (1883) showed how Europeans could block equality. Banerjee's **Indian National Conference** (1883) and Hume's **Indian National Union** (1884) were the last steps before the Congress.

#### Political associations before 1885

| Association | Year / place | Founders and notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha** | **1836**, Calcutta | Associates of **Rammohan Roy**; earliest political body |
| **Landholders' Society** | **1837**, Calcutta | **Dwarkanath Tagore**; zamindars of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa |
| **Bengal British India Society** | **1843** | **William Adam**, a friend of Rammohan Roy |
| **British Indian Association** | **1851**, Calcutta | Pres. **Radhakant Deb**, Secy. Debendranath Tagore; merged the two earlier bodies |
| **Madras Native Association** | **1852**, Madras | **Gajula Lakshminarasu Chetty** (a Telugu merchant); ryots' grievances; dissolved 1867 |
| **Bombay Association** | **1852**, Bombay | **Jagannath Shankarsheth** (with Naoroji) |
| **London Indian Society** | **1865**, London | Naoroji, W.C. Bonnerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta, Tyabji |
| **East India Association** | **1866**, London | **Dadabhai Naoroji**; lobbied British opinion |
| **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha** | **1870**, Pune | **M.G. Ranade**, G.V. Joshi, S.H. Chiplonkar; famine relief, mediation |
| **National Indian Association** | **1870** | **Mary Carpenter**; women's education |
| **Indian League** | **1875**, Calcutta | **Sisir Kumar Ghosh** (Amrita Bazar Patrika) |
| **Indian National Association** (Indian Association) | **1876**, Calcutta | **Surendranath Banerjee** & Ananda Mohan Bose; ICS age agitation |
| **Indian National Conference** | **1883**, Calcutta | Surendranath Banerjee; **merged with the INC in 1886** |
| **Madras Mahajan Sabha** | **1884**, Madras | **M. Veeraraghavachariar**, G. Subramania Iyer, P. Ananda Charlu |
| **Bombay Presidency Association** | **1885**, Bombay | Pherozeshah Mehta, **K.T. Telang**, Badruddin Tyabji; after the Ilbert Bill row |
| **Indian National Union** | **1884** | **A.O. Hume**; renamed **Indian National Congress** (Naoroji's suggestion) |

#### The background — Lytton and Ripon

| Measure | Year / Viceroy | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| **Vernacular Press Act** | **1878**, Lytton | '**Gagging Act**' on Indian-language papers; repealed by Ripon (**1882**) |
| **Arms Act** | **1878**, Lytton | Indians needed a **licence** to carry arms; Europeans exempt |
| **ICS age cut** | **1876**, Lytton | Maximum age **21 to 19** — Indian Association protested |
| **Delhi Durbar** | **1877**, Lytton | Victoria proclaimed **Kaisar-i-Hind** during a famine |
| **Ilbert Bill** | **1883**, Ripon | Indian judges could try Europeans; white backlash → compromise (half-European jury) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Indian Association (1876)** = S.N. Banerjee; **Indian League (1875)** = Sisir Kumar Ghosh; **Indian National Conference (1883)** = Banerjee again, merged in 1886.
- **East India Association** was in **London**, not Calcutta.

**TL;DR**
- Calcutta: Landholders' Society 1837 → British Indian Association 1851 → Indian Association 1876.
- Bombay/London: East India Association 1866; Poona Sarvajanik Sabha 1870; Bombay Presidency Association 1885.
- Madras: Madras Native Association 1852 (Lakshminarasu Chetty); Madras Mahajan Sabha 1884.
- Lytton: Vernacular Press Act and Arms Act 1878; Ripon: Ilbert Bill 1883.
keyPoints: The Madras Native Association (1852) was founded by Gajula Lakshminarasu Chetty.
The Vernacular Press Act (1878) was called the 'Gagging Act'; Ripon repealed it in 1882.
The Indian National Conference (1883) merged with the Congress in 1886.
Hume's Indian National Union (1884) was renamed the Indian National Congress.

items.title: Founding of the Congress — Detail and Debate
items.body:
### Founding of the Congress — Detail and Debate

**In one line**
The finer points of 1885: the Viceroy, the venue change, the delegates, and the debate over why Hume helped.

**The story**
When the Congress met on **28 December 1885** the Viceroy was **Lord Dufferin**, who at first tolerated it and in 1888 sneered that it represented a '**microscopic minority**'. The session had been planned for **Poona**; **cholera** moved it to Bombay. Why did a British officer, Hume, help? The '**safety valve**' answer — that he wanted a harmless outlet for anger — was argued by **Lala Lajpat Rai** in 1916. Modern historians add that the Indian founders used Hume as a '**lightning conductor**', so that officials would not crush an all-Indian body at birth. Within a year the Congress grew from 72 to **434** delegates.

#### 1885 — the details

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Viceroy in 1885** | **Lord Dufferin**; later called the Congress a "**microscopic minority**" |
| **Safety-valve theory** | Hume meant the INC to vent discontent; argued by **Lajpat Rai** (Young India, 1916) from Wedderburn's life of Hume |
| **Lightning-conductor view** | Indian founders used Hume as a **lightning conductor** so officials would not crush the body |
| **First session** | **28 December 1885**, **Gokuldas Tejpal** Sanskrit College, Bombay; 72 delegates |
| **Venue shift** | Planned for **Poona**, moved to Bombay because of **cholera** |
| **Growth** | 72 delegates (1885) → **434** (Calcutta, 1886) |
| **1886 decision** | Set up **Provincial Congress Committees** |
| **First woman speaker** | **Kadambini Ganguly** addressed the 1890 Calcutta session |
| **Bonnerjee's aims** | Friendship across regions; remove **prejudice** of race, creed, region; consolidate national unity; record educated opinion |

**Don't confuse**
- **Safety valve** (Hume's motive, argued by Lajpat Rai) ≠ **lightning conductor** (the founders' use of Hume).
- **Dufferin** was Viceroy in 1885 — not Ripon (left 1884) or Lansdowne (from 1888).

**TL;DR**
- Viceroy 1885: Dufferin ("microscopic minority").
- Safety valve: Lajpat Rai (1916); lightning conductor: Bipan Chandra's reading.
- 28 Dec 1885, Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay; Poona dropped because of cholera.
- Kadambini Ganguly addressed the 1890 session.
keyPoints: Lord Dufferin was Viceroy when the Congress was founded.
Lala Lajpat Rai put forward the 'safety valve' theory in 1916.
The first session moved from Poona to Bombay because of cholera.
Kadambini Ganguly was the first woman to address the Congress (1890).

### Congress Sessions 1885–1905 — Venue and President

**In one line**
Every annual session of the Moderate era with its venue and president; the presidents rotated between the three Presidencies and a few British friends.

**The story**
The Congress met every December in a different city so that no region felt left out. The early presidents were the leading Moderates — **W.C. Bonnerjee**, **Dadabhai Naoroji** (three times: 1886, 1893, 1906), **Surendranath Banerjee**, **Gokhale** — and sympathetic Britons such as **George Yule** (the first English president, 1888), **William Wedderburn**, the Irish MP **Alfred Webb** and **Henry Cotton**. **Badruddin Tyabji** (1887) was the first Muslim president and **P. Ananda Charlu** (Nagpur 1891) the first from Andhra. At **Calcutta 1896** 'Vande Mataram' was first sung, and at **Calcutta 1901** a young **Gandhi** first spoke from the Congress platform.

#### Sessions 1885–1905

| Year | Venue | President | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1885** | Bombay | **W.C. Bonnerjee** | First session; 72 delegates |
| **1886** | Calcutta | **Dadabhai Naoroji** | 434 delegates; National Conference merged |
| **1887** | Madras | **Badruddin Tyabji** | First Muslim president |
| **1888** | Allahabad | **George Yule** | First English president |
| **1889** | Bombay | **William Wedderburn** | — |
| **1890** | Calcutta | **Pherozeshah Mehta** | Kadambini Ganguly spoke |

| **1893** | Lahore | **Dadabhai Naoroji** | Naoroji's second term |
| **1894** | Madras | **Alfred Webb** | Irish MP |
| **1895** | Poona | **Surendranath Banerjee** | — |
| **1896** | Calcutta | **Rahimtulla M. Sayani** | Vande Mataram first sung |
| **1897** | Amraoti | **C. Sankaran Nair** | Condemned Tilak's arrest |
| **1898** | Madras | **Ananda Mohan Bose** | — |

Gokhale presided over the 1905 Benares session.

### Congress Sessions 1906–1922 — Venue and President

**In one line**
Sessions from the Swadeshi years to the end of Non-Cooperation, including the two special sessions of 1918 and 1920.

**The story**
After 1905 the venues tracked the politics. **Calcutta 1906** under Naoroji adopted '**Swaraj**'; **Surat 1907** under **Rash Behari Ghosh** broke up, and Ghosh presided again at Madras 1908. The parties reunited at **Lucknow 1916**, and **Annie Besant** became the first woman president at **Calcutta 1917**. Two **special sessions** dealt with emergencies: Bombay (August 1918, Hasan Imam) on the Montford proposals and Calcutta (September 1920, **Lala Lajpat Rai**) which first approved Non-Cooperation; the regular **Nagpur** session (December 1920) ratified it. In 1921 **Hakim Ajmal Khan** presided because C.R. Das was in jail; at **Gaya 1922** Das lost the council-entry vote.

items.title: Congress Sessions 1923–1948 — Venue and President
items.body:
### Congress Sessions 1923–1948 — Venue and President

**In one line**
The Gandhian decades: from the Delhi special session of 1923 to the first session of free India at Jaipur.

**The story**
**Abul Kalam Azad**, aged 35, became the youngest president at the Delhi special session (1923), which let the Swarajists enter the councils; three months later **Maulana Mohammad Ali** presided at **Kakinada** in Andhra, where the **Hindustani Seva Dal** was born. **Gandhi** presided only once (**Belgaum 1924**) and **Sarojini Naidu** became the first Indian woman president (**Kanpur 1925**). The **Nehrus** handed over the presidency father-to-son (Calcutta 1928 → Lahore 1929). There were **no sessions in 1930, 1935 and 1941–45** because the Congress was banned or its leaders were in jail. **Faizpur** (December 1936) was the first session in a village; **Meerut 1946** (Kripalani) was the last before freedom and **Jaipur 1948** (Pattabhi Sitaramayya) the first after it.

#### Sessions 1923–1948

|---|---|---|---|
| **1923 (Special)** | Delhi (Special, Sept) | **Abul Kalam Azad** | Youngest president; council entry allowed |

| **1928** | Calcutta | **Motilal Nehru** | Dominion-status ultimatum |
| **1929** | Lahore | **Jawaharlal Nehru** | Purna Swaraj |

items.title: Landmark Congress Sessions — What Each Decided
items.body:
### Landmark Congress Sessions — What Each Decided

**In one line**
The sessions examiners ask about are the ones that changed something: a song, a goal, a split, a constitution or a new organisation.

**The story**
Read the Congress's story through its resolutions. It started by asking for reforms (**Lucknow 1899** on the drain), took up **Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education** at **Calcutta 1906**, wrote its first **constitution** in 1908, and rebuilt itself at **Nagpur 1920** into a mass party with a **Working Committee**, **linguistic** provincial committees and a **four-anna** fee. The demand for full freedom was moved by **Hasrat Mohani** (1921), passed as a resolution at **Madras 1927**, turned into an ultimatum at **Calcutta 1928**, and finally adopted at Lahore 1929. **Karachi 1931** wrote down the rights free India would guarantee; **Haripura 1938** started national planning.

#### Resolutions and firsts

| Session | What happened |
|---|---|
| **Calcutta 1896** | **Vande Mataram** first sung (by Tagore) |
| **Lucknow 1899** | Stop the drain; permanent fixation of **land revenue** |
| **Calcutta 1901** | **Gandhi** first on the Congress platform (South African Indians) |
| **Calcutta 1906** | Four resolutions: Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, **National Education** |
| **Madras 1908** | First written **constitution** (Allahabad Convention draft) |
| **Lahore 1909** | Disapproved **separate electorates** of Morley–Minto |
| **Calcutta 1911** | **Jana Gana Mana** first sung (27 Dec) |
| **Nagpur 1920** | Swaraj by peaceful means; **CWC of 15**; **linguistic** PCCs; membership **four annas** |
| **Ahmedabad 1921** | **Hasrat Mohani** demanded complete independence |
| **Gaya 1922** | **Council-entry** plan defeated → Swaraj Party |
| **Kakinada 1923** | **Hindustani Seva Dal** founded (N.S. **Hardikar**) |
| **Madras 1927** | Complete independence resolution; boycott **Simon** Commission |
| **Calcutta 1928** | Dominion Status by **31 December 1929** or civil disobedience; **Youth Congress** |
| **Karachi 1931** | **Fundamental Rights** & **National Economic Programme**; endorsed Gandhi–Irwin Pact; mourned Bhagat Singh |
| **Bombay 1934** | Constitution amended; **khadi** compulsory for elected members |
| **Lucknow 1936** | Nehru urged **socialism** as the goal |
| **Faizpur 1936** | First session in a **village** (Maharashtra) |
| **Haripura 1938** | **National Planning Committee** (Nehru chairman); support to princely-state agitations |
| **Tripuri 1939** | Bose resigned; **Rajendra Prasad** became president |
| **Meerut 1946** | **Last session** before independence (Kripalani) |

#### Records

| Person / item | Record |
|---|---|
| **Dadabhai Naoroji** | President **three times** (1886, 1893, 1906) |
| **Abul Kalam Azad** | **Youngest** president (1923, aged 35) |
| **George Yule** | **First English** president (1888) |
| **Nellie Sengupta** | **Third woman** president (1933), English-born |
| **Gap years** | No sessions in 1930, 1935 and **1941–45** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Vande Mataram** first sung **1896**; **Jana Gana Mana** first sung **1911** — both at Calcutta.
- The source PDF credits Gaya 1922 with setting up the Working Committee; the CWC was created at **Nagpur 1920**. It also places the Lucknow Pact at Karachi 1913 — the Pact was signed at **Lucknow in 1916**.

**TL;DR**
- Calcutta 1896: Vande Mataram; Calcutta 1901: Gandhi; Calcutta 1906: four resolutions; Calcutta 1911: Jana Gana Mana.
- Nagpur 1920: CWC of 15, linguistic PCCs, four-anna membership.
- Independence: Hasrat Mohani 1921 → Madras 1927 resolution → Calcutta 1928 ultimatum → Lahore 1929.
- Karachi 1931: Fundamental Rights; Faizpur 1936: first village session; Haripura 1938: National Planning Committee.
keyPoints: Calcutta 1906 passed the Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education resolutions.
Nagpur 1920 created a 15-member Working Committee and linguistic PCCs.
Hasrat Mohani first demanded complete independence at Ahmedabad (1921).
The Hindustani Seva Dal was founded at the Kakinada session (1923).
Dadabhai Naoroji presided three times; Azad was the youngest president.

items.title: The Moderates in Detail — Leaders, Demands and the 1892 Act
items.body:
### The Moderates in Detail — Leaders, Demands and the 1892 Act

**In one line**
The early Congress leaders believed British rule could be reformed by argument; their real legacy was the economic critique of the Raj.

**The story**
The Moderates (1885–1905) were lawyers, journalists and scholars. **Dadabhai Naoroji**, the '**Grand Old Man**', became the first Indian MP (**Finsbury** Central, 1892) and showed in **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India** how wealth was drained to Britain; **R.C. Dutt**'s **Economic History of India** backed him with figures. **Gokhale**, a disciple of **Ranade**, founded the **Servants of India Society** in 1905. **Surendranath Banerjee** ran **The Bengalee**. Their demands were modest — **simultaneous** ICS exams in India, cuts in **military** spending, larger councils — and their one gain was the **Indian Councils Act 1892**, which let members discuss the budget. Younger men mocked all this as '**political mendicancy**'.

#### Moderate leaders and ideas

| Leader / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Dadabhai Naoroji** | '**Grand Old Man** of India'; first Indian MP (1892, **Finsbury** Central, Liberal) |
| **Naoroji's book** | **Poverty and Un-British Rule** in India (1901) — the Drain of Wealth |
| **R.C. Dutt** | **Economic History of India** (economic critique); ICS officer; president 1899 |
| **G.K. Gokhale** | Founded **Servants of India Society** (**1905**); political guru of Gandhi |
| **M.G. Ranade** | Political guru of **Gokhale**; Poona Sarvajanik Sabha |
| **Surendranath Banerjee** | Edited **The Bengalee**; called **Rashtraguru**; removed from the ICS |
| **Pherozeshah Mehta** | Bombay Municipal Corporation; founded **Bombay Chronicle** (1913) |
| **Dinshaw Wacha** | Moderate economist — **currency**, public debt |
| **Indian Councils Act 1892** | Larger councils; indirect election (nomination on recommendation); members could discuss the **budget**, not vote |
| **Critique** | '**Political mendicancy**' / 'tea-party politics'; the 3 Ps — prayer, petition, protest |
| **Demands** | **Simultaneous** ICS exams in India; separate executive & judiciary; cut **military** spending; expand councils |
| **Social base** | **Educated** urban **middle class**; Extremists reached students and lower-middle classes |

**Don't confuse**
- **Gokhale's guru = Ranade**; **Gandhi's guru = Gokhale**.
- The **1892 Act** allowed budget **discussion** only; budget **voting** came only partly with the 1919 Act.

**TL;DR**
- Naoroji: Grand Old Man, first Indian MP (Finsbury 1892), Poverty and Un-British Rule (1901).
- R.C. Dutt: Economic History of India.
- Gokhale: Servants of India Society 1905; Ranade his guru.
- Indian Councils Act 1892: budget discussion, indirect election.
keyPoints: Dadabhai Naoroji was elected to the British Parliament from Finsbury Central in 1892.
R.C. Dutt wrote The Economic History of India.
Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in 1905.
The Indian Councils Act 1892 let members discuss the budget.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society (1905).

items.title: Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi Movement — Detail
items.body:
### Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi Movement — Detail

**In one line**
Curzon split Bengal in 1905; Bengal answered with Swadeshi — boycott, national schools, Indian industry and new art — until the partition was undone in 1911.

**The story**
The partition was announced in July 1905 and came into force on **16 October 1905**, creating **Eastern Bengal and Assam** with its capital at **Dacca**. Bengalis had already proclaimed **boycott** at the Calcutta **Town Hall** on **7 August 1905**. On the partition day they fasted, tied rakhis (**Raksha Bandhan**) and sang Tagore's **Amar Sonar Bangla**. Swadeshi built its own institutions — the **National Council of Education** (1906) and the **Bengal National College** — and its own industries, such as **P.C. Ray**'s **Bengal Chemicals** and **V.O. Chidambaram Pillai**'s shipping line at **Tuticorin**. Volunteer **Samitis** carried it to villages. The movement faded by **1908**, but the British gave in at the Delhi Durbar of **12 December 1911** and moved the capital to **Delhi**.

#### Swadeshi — dates, people and institutions

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Announced / effective** | Announced July 1905; came into force **16 October 1905** (Curzon) |
| **New provinces** | **Eastern Bengal and Assam** (capital **Dacca**, Muslim majority) and Bengal (Calcutta) |
| **Swadeshi proclaimed** | Boycott resolution at Calcutta **Town Hall**, **7 August 1905** |
| **16 Oct 1905** | Day of mourning; **Raksha Bandhan** unity; Tagore's **Amar Sonar Bangla** |
| **Annulment** | Delhi Durbar of George V, **12 December 1911**; capital shifted Calcutta → **Delhi** (Hardinge II) |
| **National Council of Education** | 15 Aug 1906; **Bengal National College** (Aurobindo principal); Bengal Technical Institute |
| **V.O. Chidambaram Pillai** | **Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company**, **Tuticorin** (1906) |
| **P.C. Ray** | **Bengal Chemicals** — Swadeshi industry |
| **Ashwini Kumar Dutta** | **Swadesh Bandhab Samiti**, **Barisal** |
| **Abanindranath Tagore** | Painted **Bharat Mata** |
| **Regional spread** | Punjab: Lajpat Rai & **Ajit Singh**; Delhi: **Syed Haider Raza**; Madras: V.O.C.; Maharashtra: Tilak; Andhra: Vandemataram |
| **Samitis** | Volunteer **Samitis** — Swadesh Bandhab, Brati, Suhrid, Anushilan — the backbone of Swadeshi |
| **Decline** | Did not reach most **Muslim peasants**; faded by **1908** (repression, Surat split, no leaders) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Announced** July 1905 ≠ **effective** 16 October 1905 ≠ **annulled** 12 December 1911.
- The **capital shift to Delhi** was announced in 1911 (formal inauguration of New Delhi was 1931).

**TL;DR**
- Partition effective 16 Oct 1905; Eastern Bengal and Assam, capital Dacca.
- Boycott resolution: Calcutta Town Hall, 7 Aug 1905.
- National Council of Education (1906) → Bengal National College (Aurobindo).
- Annulled 12 Dec 1911; capital to Delhi.
keyPoints: The Partition of Bengal took effect on 16 October 1905.
The boycott resolution was passed at the Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905.
V.O. Chidambaram Pillai founded the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin.
The partition was annulled on 12 December 1911.

items.title: The Extremist Leaders — Papers, Titles and Prisons
items.body:
### The Extremist Leaders — Papers, Titles and Prisons

**In one line**
Lal, Bal, Pal and Aurobindo demanded Swaraj outright and took politics to the streets, festivals and newspapers.

**The story**
The Extremists ('neo-nationalists') rose because the Moderates had won little, because famine and plague (1896–97) were mishandled, and because little **Japan** had beaten **Russia** in 1905. **Tilak** used his papers **Kesari** and **Mahratta** and the **Ganapati** and **Shivaji** festivals to reach ordinary people; Valentine **Chirol** called him the '**Father of Indian Unrest**'. Jailed in **Mandalay** (1908–14), he wrote **Gita Rahasya**. **Lala Lajpat Rai**, '**Punjab Kesari**', was deported in 1907 with **Ajit Singh**. **Bipin Chandra Pal** preached boycott in Bengal, and **Aurobindo Ghosh**, editor of **Bande Mataram**, gave the theory of passive resistance before retiring to **Pondicherry**.

#### Extremist leaders

| Leader / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Tilak — papers** | **Kesari** (Marathi) & **Mahratta** (English), from 1881 |
| **Tilak — festivals** | **Ganapati** utsav (1893), **Shivaji** festival (1895) |
| **Tilak — title** | '**Father of Indian Unrest**' (Valentine **Chirol**); 'Lokmanya' |
| **Tilak — prison** | **Mandalay** 1908–14; wrote **Gita Rahasya**; also The Arctic Home of the Vedas |
| **Tilak — 1897** | First **sedition** trial (1897, plague-measure writings) |
| **Lala Lajpat Rai** | '**Punjab Kesari**'; deported to Mandalay with **Ajit Singh** (1907); DAV schools; Punjab National Bank |
| **Lajpat Rai abroad** | **Indian Home Rule League of America** (New York, Oct 1917) |
| **Lajpat Rai — society** | **Servants of the People Society** (1921, Lahore) |
| **Bipin Chandra Pal** | 'Father of **Revolutionary Thoughts**'; edited New India, Paridarshak; The Soul of India |
| **Aurobindo Ghosh** | English daily **Bande Mataram**; doctrine of passive resistance; acquitted in Alipore case; **Pondicherry** 1910 (ashram 1926) |
| **Lal-Bal-Pal** | Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Tilak (Maharashtra), Pal (Bengal) |
| **Why Extremism rose** | **Japan** beat **Russia** (1905); 1896–97 famine & plague; Curzon's measures; Moderate failures |
| **Curzon's other measures** | Calcutta Corporation Act 1899; **Official Secrets** Act 1904; **Indian Universities Act** 1904 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Punjab Kesari** = Lajpat Rai; **Kesari** (paper) = Tilak; **Andhra Kesari** = T. Prakasam.
- Aurobindo's **Bande Mataram** (Calcutta daily, 1905–08) ≠ Madame Cama's **Bande Mataram** (Paris).

**TL;DR**
- Tilak: Kesari & Mahratta; Ganapati 1893, Shivaji 1895; Mandalay 1908–14 (Gita Rahasya).
- Lajpat Rai: Punjab Kesari; deported 1907 with Ajit Singh.
- Bipin Pal: Father of Revolutionary Thoughts; Aurobindo: Bande Mataram, Pondicherry 1910.
- Spur: Japan defeated Russia (1905).
keyPoints: Valentine Chirol called Tilak the 'Father of Indian Unrest'.
Tilak wrote Gita Rahasya in Mandalay jail.
Lala Lajpat Rai, 'Punjab Kesari', was deported with Ajit Singh in 1907.
Aurobindo Ghosh edited the English daily Bande Mataram.

items.title: Muslim League, Morley–Minto and the Surat Split — Detail
items.body:
### Muslim League, Morley–Minto and the Surat Split — Detail

**In one line**
In 1906–09 the British met nationalism with a carrot for Muslims (separate electorates) and a stick for Extremists, while the Congress itself broke at Surat.

**The story**
On **1 October 1906** a deputation led by the **Aga Khan** met Lord Minto at **Simla** and asked for separate Muslim seats; three months later the **Muslim League** was born at **Dacca** under **Nawab Salimullah**. The **Indian Councils Act 1909**, named after **John Morley** and Lord Minto, granted **separate electorates**, enlarged the councils to **60** additional members and made **S.P. Sinha** the first Indian on the Viceroy's **Executive Council**. Meanwhile at **Surat** (December 1907) the Moderates, backing **Rash Behari Ghosh**, clashed with the Extremists over the **1906 resolutions**; shoes flew and the session broke up. The Moderates' **Allahabad Convention** (1908) shut the Extremists out, and the **Seditious Meetings** and **Press** Acts silenced them.

#### 1906–1910 — League, reforms and split

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Simla Deputation** | **1 Oct 1906**; led by the **Aga Khan** to Minto; asked for separate electorates |
| **Muslim League founded** | Dacca, **30 Dec 1906**; **Nawab Salimullah**; first president the Aga Khan |
| **Jinnah** | Joined the League in **1913** (kept Congress membership) |
| **Morley–Minto 1909** | **Separate electorates** for Muslims; Minto = "**father of communal electorate**" |
| **S.P. Sinha** | First Indian in the Viceroy's **Executive Council** (Law Member, 1909) |
| **Names** | **John Morley** (Secretary of State) & Lord Minto (Viceroy) |
| **Council size** | Imperial Council additional members 16 → **60**; members could move **resolutions**, ask supplementaries |
| **Surat Split** | Moderates (Rash Behari Ghosh as president) vs Extremists (wanted Lajpat Rai/Tilak; keep the **1906 resolutions**) |
| **After Surat** | **Allahabad Convention** (1908) — constitution kept Extremists out until 1916 |
| **Repression** | **Seditious Meetings** Act 1907; Newspapers Act 1908; **Indian Press Act** 1910 |

**Don't confuse**
- Separate electorates began in **1909**; the Congress **accepted** them in the **Lucknow Pact (1916)**; **1919** extended them to Sikhs and others.
- **Simla Deputation (1906)** ≠ **Simla Conference (1945)**.

**TL;DR**
- Simla Deputation 1 Oct 1906 (Aga Khan); League founded Dacca 30 Dec 1906 (Salimullah).
- Morley–Minto 1909: separate electorates; 60 members; S.P. Sinha Law Member.
- Surat 1907: split over president (Rash Behari Ghosh) and 1906 resolutions.
- Allahabad Convention 1908; Seditious Meetings Act 1907; Indian Press Act 1910.
keyPoints: The Simla Deputation (1906) was led by the Aga Khan.
The Muslim League was founded at Dacca in 1906 under Nawab Salimullah.
Minto is called the father of communal electorate.
S.P. Sinha was the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council.

items.title: Home Rule Leagues and the Lucknow Pact — Detail
items.body:
### Home Rule Leagues and the Lucknow Pact — Detail

**In one line**
In 1916 two Home Rule Leagues revived the national movement during the First World War, and the Lucknow Pact united the Congress, the Extremists and the League.

**The story**
With Tilak back from **Mandalay** and the Congress weak, the **Irish** idea of Home Rule caught on. **Tilak** started his League in **April 1916** at **Belgaum**; **Annie Besant** started hers in **September 1916** at **Adyar**, Madras, and spread it through her papers **New India** and **Commonweal**. The two Leagues split the country between them so as not to compete. The government **interned** Besant in **June 1917**, but the outcry freed her, and **Montagu** announced on **20 August 1917** that **responsible government** would come by stages. At **Lucknow** (December 1916) the Extremists were **readmitted**, and in the **Lucknow Pact** the Congress **accepted separate electorates** in return for a joint demand — the work of **Tilak and Jinnah**.

#### Home Rule and Lucknow

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Tilak's League** | **April 1916**, **Belgaum**; Maharashtra (minus Bombay city), Karnataka, CP & Berar; 6 branches |
| **Besant's League** | **September 1916**, Madras (**Adyar**); rest of India; ~200 branches |
| **Besant — papers** | **New India** and **Commonweal** |
| **Model** | The **Irish** Home Rule movement |
| **Repression** | Besant **interned** in **June 1917**, released in Sept; president at Calcutta 1917 |
| **August Declaration** | Montagu, **20 August 1917** — gradual **responsible government** |
| **Members** | **Jinnah**, Motilal & Jawaharlal Nehru, Sapru, Lajpat Rai; its **network** was used for the Rowlatt Satyagraha |
| **Lucknow Pact** | Dec 1916; Congress **accepted separate electorates**; joint scheme of reforms; **Tilak and Jinnah** |
| **Reunion** | Lucknow 1916 **readmitted** the Extremists (A.C. Mazumdar, president) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Tilak's** League came **first** (April 1916, Belgaum); **Besant's** in **September** (Madras).
- The Lucknow Pact **accepted** separate electorates — it did not abolish them.

**TL;DR**
- Tilak: April 1916, Belgaum; Besant: September 1916, Adyar (New India, Commonweal).
- Besant interned June 1917; August Declaration 20 Aug 1917.
- Lucknow 1916: Extremists readmitted; Lucknow Pact (Tilak–Jinnah) accepted separate electorates.
keyPoints: Tilak's Home Rule League was founded at Belgaum in April 1916.
Annie Besant's League was founded in September 1916 at Adyar, Madras.
Montagu's August Declaration (20 August 1917) promised responsible government.
In the Lucknow Pact the Congress accepted separate electorates.

items.title: Revolutionaries, First Phase (1897–1918) — India and Abroad
items.body:
### Revolutionaries, First Phase (1897–1918) — India and Abroad

**In one line**
Alongside Swadeshi a minority of young men chose bombs and pistols; abroad, Indians organised from London, Paris, Berlin, San Francisco and Kabul.

**The story**
Revolutionary terrorism began with the **Chapekar** brothers, who killed the hated plague officer **Rand** at Poona in 1897. In Maharashtra **Savarkar** built **Abhinav Bharat**; in Bengal the **Anushilan Samiti** (1902) and the **Yugantar** group of **Barindra** Ghosh trained youths. The **Muzaffarpur** bomb of 1908, meant for **Kingsford**, sent **Khudiram Bose** to the gallows and led to the **Alipore** Bomb Case. Abroad, **Shyamji Krishna Varma**'s **India House** in London produced **Madan Lal Dhingra**, who killed **Curzon Wyllie**; **Madame Cama** raised a flag at **Stuttgart**. In America the **Ghadar Party** (1913) of **Sohan Singh Bhakna** and Har Dayal planned a rising for February 1915, and **Rash Behari Bose** had already bombed Viceroy **Hardinge** in Delhi (1912). The **Komagata Maru** and the **Kabul** government of **Mahendra Pratap** belong to the same war-time hope.

#### First-phase revolutionaries

| Person / event | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Chapekar brothers** | Shot plague commissioner **Rand** (and Lt. Ayerst), Poona **1897** |
| **Abhinav Bharat** | **V.D. Savarkar** — Mitra Mela 1899 → **Abhinav Bharat** 1904 (Nasik) |
| **Anushilan Samiti** | Calcutta **1902**, **Pramatha Mitra**; Dacca branch Pulin Behari Das |
| **Yugantar** | Weekly (1906) of **Barindra** Kumar Ghosh & Bhupendranath Dutta → Jugantar group |
| **Muzaffarpur bomb** | **30 April 1908**; **Khudiram Bose** & Prafulla Chaki; target judge **Kingsford** (killed two Englishwomen) |

items.title: Revolutionaries, Second Phase (1924–1940) — HRA, HSRA, Chittagong
items.body:
### Revolutionaries, Second Phase (1924–1940) — HRA, HSRA, Chittagong

**In one line**
After Non-Cooperation was called off, young men turned again to revolutionary action, now with a socialist goal.

**The story**
The **Hindustan Republican Association** (Kanpur, 1924) of **Sachindranath Sanyal** and Ramprasad Bismil funded itself by looting a government train at **Kakori** (9 August 1925); four of its men, including **Ashfaqullah Khan**, were hanged. At **Feroz Shah Kotla**, Delhi (September 1928), **Chandrashekhar Azad** and **Bhagat Singh** renamed it the **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association**. They shot **Saunders** at Lahore (December 1928) to avenge Lajpat Rai, and on **8 April 1929** Bhagat Singh and **Batukeshwar Dutt** threw harmless bombs in the Central Assembly and courted arrest. **Jatin Das** died on the **64**th day of his fast; Bhagat Singh, **Sukhdev** and Rajguru were hanged on **23 March 1931**, a month after Azad fell at **Alfred Park**. In Bengal **Surya Sen** raided the **Chittagong** armoury (18 April 1930) with young women like **Pritilata Waddedar**; in London **Udham Singh** shot **O'Dwyer** in 1940.

#### Second-phase revolutionaries

| Person / event | Fact |
|---|---|
| **HRA** | Kanpur, Oct **1924**; **Sachindranath Sanyal**, Ramprasad Bismil, Jogesh Chatterjee |
| **Kakori train action** | **9 August 1925**, near Lucknow |
| **Kakori martyrs** | Bismil, **Ashfaqullah Khan**, **Rajendra Lahiri**, Roshan Singh hanged (1927) |
| **Ramprasad Bismil** | '**Sarfaroshi** ki Tamanna' |
| **HSRA** | **Feroz Shah Kotla**, Delhi, Sept 1928 — **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association**; Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev |
| **Naujawan Bharat Sabha** | Lahore **1926**, Bhagat Singh |
| **Saunders killing** | Lahore, **17 December 1928**; Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Azad (meant for Scott) |
| **Assembly bomb** | **8 April 1929**; Bhagat Singh & **Batukeshwar Dutt**; against Public Safety & Trade Disputes Bills; "Inquilab Zindabad" |
| **Jatin Das** | Died on day **64** of a hunger strike, Lahore jail, Sept 1929 |
| **Execution** | **23 March 1931**, Lahore — Bhagat Singh, **Sukhdev**, Rajguru (Shaheed Diwas) |
| **Chandrashekhar Azad** | Died at **Alfred Park**, Allahabad, **27 February 1931** |
| **Bhagat Singh — writing** | '**Why I Am an Atheist**' (1930) |
| **Chittagong Armoury Raid** | **18 April 1930**; **Surya Sen** (Masterda); Indian Republican Army |
| **Chittagong women** | **Pritilata Waddedar** (Pahartali club attack, 1932) & **Kalpana Dutt** |
| **Surya Sen** | Captured 1933, hanged **January 1934** |
| **Writers' Building** | Dec 1930 — **Benoy**, Badal, Dinesh shot IG Simpson |
| **Bina Das** | Fired at Governor **Stanley Jackson** (1932 convocation) |
| **Udham Singh** | Shot Michael **O'Dwyer**, Caxton Hall, London, 13 March 1940 |
| **Meerut Conspiracy Case** | 1929 — 31 communist and trade-union leaders tried |

**Don't confuse**
- **Saunders** was killed (Dec 1928) by mistake for **Scott**, who ordered the lathi-charge on Lajpat Rai.
- **Udham Singh** shot **Michael O'Dwyer** (Lt-Governor), not General Dyer (who died in 1927).

**TL;DR**
- HRA 1924 (Sanyal, Bismil) → Kakori 9 Aug 1925 → HSRA 1928 (Feroz Shah Kotla, Azad).
- Saunders 17 Dec 1928; Assembly bombs 8 Apr 1929 (Bhagat Singh, B.K. Dutt).
- Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru hanged 23 Mar 1931; Azad died Alfred Park 27 Feb 1931.
- Chittagong 18 Apr 1930 (Surya Sen); Udham Singh shot O'Dwyer 1940.
keyPoints: The Kakori train action took place on 9 August 1925.
The HSRA was formed at Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi, in 1928.
Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt bombed the Central Assembly on 8 April 1929.
Surya Sen led the Chittagong Armoury Raid on 18 April 1930.
Udham Singh shot Michael O'Dwyer in London in 1940.

items.title: 1919 — The Montford Act, the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh
items.body:
### 1919 — The Montford Act, the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh

**In one line**
In one year the British offered limited self-rule with one hand (the 1919 Act) and took away civil liberty with the other (the Rowlatt Act); Amritsar turned Indians against the Raj.

**The story**
The **Montagu–Chelmsford** Report (1918) became the **Government of India Act 1919**. It brought **dyarchy** to the provinces — **transferred** subjects like education went to elected ministers, **reserved** subjects like police stayed with the governor — made the centre **bicameral** (**Council of State** and Assembly), and extended separate seats to **Sikhs**, Christians and **Anglo-Indians**. But in March 1919 the **Rowlatt Act** (the **Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act**) allowed detention without trial — '**no vakil**, no daleel, no appeal'. Gandhi's **Satyagraha Sabha** called a hartal on **6 April**. When **Kitchlew** and **Satyapal** were arrested at Amritsar, a crowd met at Jallianwala Bagh on **Baisakhi**, **13 April 1919**, and Dyer fired into it. The **Hunter Committee** inquired; **Tagore** gave up his **knighthood**.

#### 1919

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Montford Report** | **Montagu–Chelmsford** Report, **1918** → GoI Act 1919 |
| **Dyarchy** | Provinces: **reserved** (governor) vs **transferred** (ministers) subjects |
| **Centre** | **Bicameral**: **Council of State** + Legislative Assembly; direct elections; ~10% propertied franchise |
| **Communal seats** | Extended to **Sikhs**, Indian Christians, **Anglo-Indians**, Europeans |
| **New offices** | **High Commissioner** in London; Public Service Commission (**1926**); statutory commission after 10 years |
| **Rowlatt Act** | March 1919, **Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act**; Sedition Committee of Justice **Sidney Rowlatt** |
| **Popular slogan** | '**No vakil**, no daleel, no appeal' — detention without trial |
| **Rowlatt Satyagraha** | All-India hartal **6 April 1919**; **Satyagraha Sabha** (Bombay) |
| **Amritsar arrests** | **Saifuddin Kitchlew** & Dr **Satyapal** (10 Apr 1919) |
| **Jallianwala Bagh** | **13 April 1919** (**Baisakhi**); Gen. Dyer; official toll 379; Lt-Governor Michael O'Dwyer |
| **Hunter Committee** | Disorders Inquiry Committee, Oct 1919 (Lord William Hunter); Congress held its own inquiry |
| **Protests** | Tagore renounced **knighthood**; Gandhi returned **Kaiser-i-Hind**; Sankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Council |

**Don't confuse**
- **Dyarchy** of 1919 = in the **provinces**; the 1935 Act **abolished** it there and proposed it at the **Centre**.
- **Rowlatt** = Sedition Committee judge; **Hunter** = Jallianwala inquiry; **Dyer** fired; **O'Dwyer** was Lt-Governor.

**TL;DR**
- GoI Act 1919: provincial dyarchy, bicameral centre, direct elections, communal seats extended.
- Rowlatt Act Mar 1919; hartal 6 Apr 1919 (Satyagraha Sabha).
- Jallianwala 13 Apr 1919 (Baisakhi, Dyer); Hunter Committee; Tagore renounced knighthood.
keyPoints: The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
The Rowlatt Act was officially the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act.
The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on Baisakhi, 13 April 1919.
Tagore renounced his knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh.

items.title: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (1919–22) — Detail
items.body:
### Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (1919–22) — Detail

**In one line**
Gandhi joined the Khilafat grievance to the Punjab wrongs and the demand for Swaraj, producing the first all-India mass movement.

**The story**
The **Khilafat Committee** of the Ali brothers (**Shaukat Ali** and Mohammad Ali) protested Britain's treatment of the Turkish Caliph; **Khilafat Day** was kept on **17 October 1919**. Non-Cooperation formally began on **1 August 1920**, the day **Tilak died**. Its programme was to **surrender titles** and boycott schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth, and to build substitutes — **Jamia Millia Islamia**, **Kashi Vidyapith** and others. The **Tilak Swaraj Fund** passed its ₹1 crore target; the Bezawada AICC (1921) asked for **20 lakh** charkhas. The **Prince of Wales** (November 1921) was greeted with a hartal. Then at **Chauri Chaura** (**Gorakhpur**) on **4 February 1922** a crowd burnt a police station; by the **Bardoli resolution** (12 February) Gandhi called the movement off. **Atatürk**'s abolition of the Caliphate (1924) ended the Khilafat cause.

#### Khilafat and Non-Cooperation

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Khilafat Committee** | 1919; Ali brothers (Mohammad & **Shaukat Ali**), Azad, Ajmal Khan, Hasrat Mohani |
| **Khilafat Day** | **17 October 1919**; Gandhi presided over the Khilafat Conference, Delhi, Nov 1919 |
| **Launch** | **1 August 1920** (the day **Tilak died**) |
| **Tilak Swaraj Fund** | ₹1 crore; Bezawada AICC (Mar–Apr 1921): 1 crore members, **20 lakh** charkhas |
| **Prince of Wales** | Arrived Bombay 17 Nov 1921 — hartal and boycott |
| **National institutions** | **Jamia Millia Islamia** (1920), **Kashi Vidyapith**, Gujarat Vidyapith, Bihar Vidyapith |
| **Programme** | **Surrender titles**; boycott schools, courts, councils, foreign cloth; khadi; Hindu–Muslim unity |
| **Chauri Chaura** | **4 February 1922**, **Gorakhpur** district; 22 policemen killed |
| **Withdrawal** | **Bardoli resolution**, **12 February 1922** |
| **Gandhi jailed** | March 1922, **six years** (Judge **Broomfield**); released 1924 |
| **End of Khilafat** | Mustafa Kemal **Atatürk** abolished the Caliphate (**1924**) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Chauri Chaura** was on **4 February 1922** (some books print 5 February); the **Bardoli resolution** of withdrawal was **12 February 1922**.
- **Bardoli resolution (1922)** ≠ **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928, Patel)**.

**TL;DR**
- Khilafat: Ali brothers; Khilafat Day 17 Oct 1919.
- NCM began 1 Aug 1920 (Tilak died); Tilak Swaraj Fund ₹1 crore.
- Institutions: Jamia Millia, Kashi, Gujarat, Bihar Vidyapiths.
- Chauri Chaura 4 Feb 1922 → Bardoli resolution 12 Feb 1922.
keyPoints: Non-Cooperation formally began on 1 August 1920, the day Tilak died.
Jamia Millia Islamia was a national institution of Non-Cooperation.
Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur) took place on 4 February 1922.
The Bardoli resolution of 12 February 1922 withdrew Non-Cooperation.

items.title: Swarajists, No-changers and the Left (1923–1934)
items.body:
### Swarajists, No-changers and the Left (1923–1934)

**In one line**
After 1922 the Congress divided over entering the councils, and new socialist, communist and labour forces appeared.

**The story**
With Gandhi in jail, **C.R. Das** and **Motilal Nehru** founded the Swaraj Party on **1 January 1923** to enter the councils and wreck them from within; the '**No-changers**' — **Rajagopalachari**, Patel, Rajendra Prasad — stuck to constructive work. The Swarajists won seats in 1923, and in 1925 **Vithalbhai Patel** became the first Indian President of the Central Assembly; the **Muddiman** Committee looked at dyarchy. The party faded after Das died in **June 1925**. On the left, the **AITUC** (1920) organised workers under **Lajpat Rai**, **M.N. Roy** started the CPI at **Tashkent**, and in **1934** **Narendra Dev** and Jayaprakash Narayan set up the **Congress Socialist Party** inside the Congress.

#### Swarajists and the left

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Swaraj Party** | **1 January 1923**; C.R. Das (president), **Motilal Nehru** (secretary) |
| **No-changers** | Opposed council entry: Patel, Rajendra Prasad, **Rajagopalachari**, Ansari |
| **Vithalbhai Patel** | First Indian President of the Central Legislative Assembly (**1925**) |
| **Muddiman Committee** | 1924 — reviewed dyarchy |
| **Decline** | C.R. Das died **June 1925**; party split |
| **All India Trade Union Congress** (AITUC) | Bombay **1920**; first president Lala Lajpat Rai; N.M. Joshi |
| **CPI** | **M.N. Roy**, **Tashkent** 1920; Kanpur conference 1925 |
| **Congress Socialist Party** | **1934** — Acharya **Narendra Dev**, Jayaprakash Narayan |
| **Labour laws** | **Trade Union Act 1926**; Trade Disputes Act 1929 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Vithalbhai Patel** (Assembly President 1925) is the elder brother of **Vallabhbhai Patel** (a No-changer).
- **AITUC 1920** (Lajpat Rai) ≠ **All India Kisan Sabha 1936** (Sahajanand).

**TL;DR**
- Swaraj Party 1 Jan 1923 (Das, Motilal); No-changers: Rajaji, Patel, Prasad, Ansari.
- Vithalbhai Patel: first Indian Assembly President, 1925.
- AITUC 1920 (Lajpat Rai); CPI Tashkent 1920 (M.N. Roy); CSP 1934 (Narendra Dev, JP).
keyPoints: The Swaraj Party was founded on 1 January 1923.
Vithalbhai Patel was the first Indian President of the Central Legislative Assembly.
The AITUC was founded in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as president.
The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934.

items.title: Simon Commission, Nehru Report and the Lahore Session — Detail
items.body:
### Simon Commission, Nehru Report and the Lahore Session — Detail

**In one line**
An all-white commission, an Indian answer in the Nehru Report, a Muslim counter-answer and finally the Purna Swaraj resolution.

**The story**
Secretary of State **Birkenhead** announced in November 1927 a seven-man commission under Sir John Simon — every member, including the future PM **Attlee**, was British. It landed on **3 February 1928** to cries of '**Simon Go Back**'. At Lahore **Lajpat Rai** was beaten and died on **17 November 1928**. Indians replied with the **Nehru Report** (August 1928), which asked for **Dominion Status** and **joint electorates**; **Jinnah**'s **Fourteen Points** (1929) rejected it, and Nehru and Bose's **Independence for India League** wanted more. Irwin's **Deepavali Declaration** (31 October 1929) came too late: on the **Ravi** at midnight on **31 December 1929** the tricolour went up, and **26 January 1930** was kept as Independence Day. Gandhi then sent Irwin **Eleven Demands**, starting with the **salt tax**.

#### 1927–1930

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Simon Commission** | Announced Nov 1927 (**Birkenhead**); 7 British MPs incl. **Attlee**; no Indian |
| **Arrival** | Bombay, **3 February 1928**; "**Simon Go Back**" |
| **Lajpat Rai** | Lathi-charged Lahore 30 Oct 1928; died **17 November 1928** |
| **Simon Report** | 1930 — **abolishing dyarchy**; provincial autonomy; kept separate electorates |
| **Nehru Report** | Aug 1928; Motilal Nehru; **Dominion Status**, **joint electorates** with reserved seats, fundamental rights, linguistic provinces |
| **Committee** | Motilal Nehru (chair), Subhas Bose, **Tej Bahadur Sapru**, **Ali Imam**, M.S. Aney, Mangal Singh |
| **Jinnah's reply** | **Fourteen Points**, March 1929 |
| **Young radicals** | Nehru & Bose — **Independence for India League** (1928) |
| **Irwin's offer** | **Deepavali Declaration**, 31 Oct 1929 — Dominion Status the natural goal; RTC promised |
| **Lahore** | Tricolour on the **Ravi**, midnight **31 December 1929** |
| **Independence Day** | **26 January 1930**, public **pledge** |
| **Gandhi's ultimatum** | **Eleven Demands** (Jan 1930): abolish **salt tax**, halve land revenue, cut army spending, free political prisoners |

**Don't confuse**
- **Nehru Report** (1928) = **Motilal** Nehru, Dominion Status; **Purna Swaraj** (1929) = **Jawaharlal** Nehru.
- **Simon Report** came out in **1930**, after the boycott — it fed the Round Table Conferences.

**TL;DR**
- Simon Commission: Birkenhead, 7 British MPs (Attlee); arrived 3 Feb 1928.
- Lajpat Rai died 17 Nov 1928.
- Nehru Report Aug 1928: Dominion Status, joint electorates; Jinnah's 14 Points 1929.
- Ravi flag 31 Dec 1929; Independence Day 26 Jan 1930; Eleven Demands.
keyPoints: The Simon Commission had seven British members, including Attlee.
The Nehru Report asked for Dominion Status and joint electorates.
Jinnah answered the Nehru Report with his Fourteen Points (1929).
The first Independence Day was observed on 26 January 1930.
Gandhi's Eleven Demands to Irwin (January 1930) included abolition of the salt tax — the issue that became the Dandi March.
