items.title: Civil Disobedience and the Round Table Conferences — Detail
items.body:
### Civil Disobedience and the Round Table Conferences — Detail

**In one line**
The salt march spread into a dozen local struggles; in London three conferences and a Communal Award followed.

**The story**
Gandhi walked from Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with **78** companions and picked up salt at Dandi on **6 April 1930**. The movement took local shapes: **Rajagopalachari** marched to **Vedaranyam**, **Kelappan** to **Payyanur**, **Sarojini Naidu** led the raid on **Dharasana** salt works, the **Khudai Khidmatgars** of the '**Frontier Gandhi**' rose at Peshawar where the **Garhwal Rifles** refused to fire, workers held **Sholapur**, and the Naga girl **Gaidinliu** fought in the north-east. The **First Round Table** (from 12 November 1930) met without the Congress; after the **Delhi Pact** of **5 March 1931** Gandhi went as the **sole** Congress delegate to the **Second**; the **Third** (1932) had no Congress at all. MacDonald's **Communal Award** (16 August 1932) gave the **Depressed Classes** separate seats; Gandhi's fast forced the **Poona Pact** (24 September 1932) — joint electorates with **147** reserved seats.

#### 1930–1934

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Dandi March** | Sabarmati **12 March** → Dandi **6 April 1930**; **78** marchers; ~240 miles |
| **Vedaranyam** | C. Rajagopalachari, Trichy → **Vedaranyam** |
| **Payyanur** | **K. Kelappan** (Malabar) |
| **Dharasana** | Salt works raid led by **Sarojini Naidu** (May 1930); reported by **Webb Miller** |
| **Khudai Khidmatgars** | Red Shirts of **Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan** ('**Frontier Gandhi**'), NWFP |
| **Peshawar** | **Garhwal Rifles** (Chandra Singh Garhwali) refused to fire, Qissa Khwani Bazaar, April 1930 |
| **Rani Gaidinliu** | **Naga** leader (Heraka/Zeliangrong), jailed 1932; Nehru gave the title "Rani" |
| **Sholapur** | Workers ran a parallel government (May 1930) |
| **Arrest** | Gandhi arrested **May 1930** (Yerawada jail) |
| **Gandhi–Irwin Pact** | **Delhi Pact**, **5 March 1931** |
| **First RTC** | **12 November 1930** – 19 Jan 1931; **Congress absent**; PM Ramsay MacDonald |
| **Second RTC** | Sept–Dec 1931; Gandhi the **sole** Congress delegate; deadlock on minorities |
| **Third Round Table** Conference | Nov–Dec 1932; Congress absent; **Ambedkar** and Sapru attended **all three** |
| **Second phase of CDM** | Resumed Jan 1932 (Viceroy **Willingdon**); withdrawn **1934** |
| **Communal Award** | **16 August 1932**, Ramsay MacDonald; separate electorates incl. **Depressed Classes** |
| **Poona Pact** | **24 September 1932**; joint electorate with **147** reserved seats (some sources 148; the Award had given 71); Gandhi's Yerawada fast ended |

**Don't confuse**
- **Gandhi attended only the Second RTC**; **Ambedkar** attended **all three**.
- **Communal Award** (MacDonald, 16 Aug 1932) → Gandhi's fast → **Poona Pact** (24 Sept 1932).

**TL;DR**
- Dandi: 78 marchers, 12 Mar–6 Apr 1930.
- Vedaranyam (Rajaji), Payyanur (Kelappan), Dharasana (Sarojini), Peshawar (Red Shirts, Garhwal Rifles).
- RTC-1 Nov 1930 (no Congress); Delhi Pact 5 Mar 1931; RTC-2 1931 (Gandhi sole); RTC-3 1932.
- Communal Award 16 Aug 1932; Poona Pact 24 Sept 1932 (147 seats).
keyPoints: Gandhi began the Dandi March with 78 followers.
C. Rajagopalachari led the salt march to Vedaranyam.
The Garhwal Rifles refused to fire on the Peshawar crowd in 1930.
Gandhi was the sole Congress delegate at the Second Round Table Conference.
The Poona Pact gave the Depressed Classes 147 reserved seats.

items.title: The Government of India Act 1935 and the Congress Ministries
items.body:
### The Government of India Act 1935 and the Congress Ministries

**In one line**
The 1935 Act was the British answer to the Round Tables — provincial self-government with strong safeguards; the Congress used it to govern provinces from 1937 to 1939.

**The story**
The Act — the longest Britain ever passed for India — planned an **All-India Federation** that the princes never joined, ended dyarchy in the provinces (**provincial autonomy**) and proposed it at the **Centre**. It split subjects into Federal, Provincial and **Concurrent** Lists, kept **residuary** powers with the Viceroy, created the **Federal Court** (1937) and the RBI, made **six provinces** (including **Assam**) bicameral, separated **Burma** and created Sind and **Orissa**. Nehru dismissed it as 'a machine with **strong brakes** but no engine'. Still, the Congress contested the **1937** elections, won **five provinces** outright and formed eight ministries; **Rajagopalachari** became **Premier of Madras**. When **Linlithgow** took India into the war in 1939 the ministries resigned, and the League kept a '**Day of Deliverance**'.

#### 1935 Act and 1937–39

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Federation** | **All-India Federation** of provinces + princely states — never formed (princes did not join) |
| **Autonomy** | **Provincial autonomy** (dyarchy ended in provinces); dyarchy proposed at the **Centre** |
| **Three lists** | Federal, Provincial, **Concurrent**; **residuary** powers with the Viceroy (Governor-General) |
| **Federal Court** | Set up **1937**, Delhi |
| **RBI** | **Reserve Bank of India** (1935, under the RBI Act 1934) |
| **Bicameral provinces** | **Six provinces**: Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, **Assam**, UP |
| **Map changes** | **Burma** separated (1937); Sind and **Orissa** new provinces (1936) |
| **Nehru's verdict** | 'A machine with **strong brakes** but no engine'; 'a new **charter of slavery**' |
| **Other provisions** | **Federal Public Service Commission**; separate seats for women, labour, depressed classes; ~10% franchise |
| **1937 elections** | Congress majority in **five provinces** (Madras, UP, CP, Bihar, Orissa); largest in Bombay; later ministries in NWFP & Assam (8 in all) |
| **Madras** | C. Rajagopalachari, **Premier of Madras** (1937–39) |
| **Resignation** | Oct–Nov **1939**, protest at **Linlithgow** declaring India a belligerent |
| **League's response** | **Day of Deliverance**, 22 Dec 1939 |

**Don't confuse**
- 1935: dyarchy **abolished** in provinces, **introduced** at the Centre (never worked because the federation never formed).
- **Residuary** powers: **Viceroy** in 1935; **Union** under today's Constitution.

**TL;DR**
- 1935: Federation (never formed), provincial autonomy, central dyarchy, three lists, residuary to Viceroy.
- Federal Court 1937; RBI 1935; six bicameral provinces; Burma separated.
- 1937: Congress majorities in five provinces; Rajaji Premier of Madras.
- Ministries resigned 1939 (Linlithgow); Day of Deliverance 22 Dec 1939.
keyPoints: The 1935 Act gave provincial autonomy and proposed dyarchy at the Centre.
Under the 1935 Act residuary powers lay with the Governor-General.
Six provinces were made bicameral by the 1935 Act.
Nehru called the 1935 Act 'a machine with strong brakes but no engine'.
The Muslim League celebrated 22 December 1939 as the 'Day of Deliverance'.
Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley–Minto): introduced separate electorates for Muslims, so Minto came to be called the 'father of communal electorate'.

items.title: War Years and Quit India (1939–1944) — Detail
items.body:
### War Years and Quit India (1939–1944) — Detail

**In one line**
The war forced Britain to make offers; the Congress rejected them and in 1942 told the British to quit, leaving the movement to the people once the leaders were jailed.

**The story**
Linlithgow's **August Offer** (8 August 1940) promised Dominion Status after the war; the League had already demanded separate Muslim states in the **Lahore Resolution** (23 March 1940) moved by **Fazlul Haq**. Gandhi answered with **Individual Satyagraha** from 17 October 1940 — **Vinoba Bhave** first, Nehru second. After Japan reached Burma, Churchill sent **Stafford Cripps** (March 1942) with post-war Dominion Status and the right of **provinces** to stay out — a '**post-dated cheque**'. The Working Committee met at **Wardha** (14 July 1942) and the AICC at **Gowalia Tank** (8 August) passed Quit India. '**Operation Zero Hour**' jailed every leader the next morning; **Aruna Asaf Ali** hoisted the flag, **Usha Mehta** ran a secret radio, **JP** escaped **Hazaribagh** jail, and parallel governments rose at **Ballia**, **Tamluk** and **Satara**.

#### 1940–1944

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **August Offer** | **8 August 1940**, Linlithgow: Dominion Status after the war; expanded Executive Council; War Advisory Council; minorities' veto |
| **Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution** | **23 March 1940**; moved by **Fazlul Haq**; Jinnah presided |
| **Pakistan idea** | Name coined by **Choudhary Rahmat Ali** (1933, 'Now or Never'); **Iqbal**'s Allahabad address (1930) |
| **Individual Satyagraha** | From **17 October 1940**; 1st **Vinoba Bhave**, 2nd Nehru (3rd Brahma Dutt); "Delhi Chalo" slogan |
| **Cripps Mission** | March 1942 (Churchill): post-war Dominion Status; constitution-making body; **provinces** could opt out; princes nominate |
| **Gandhi on Cripps** | 'A **post-dated cheque** (on a crashing bank)' |
| **Resolution** | CWC at **Wardha**, 14 July 1942 → AICC at **Gowalia Tank** (August Kranti Maidan), Bombay, 8 Aug 1942 |
| **Arrests** | "**Operation Zero Hour**", 9 Aug 1942; Gandhi at the **Aga Khan Palace**, Poona; CWC at Ahmednagar Fort |
| **Aruna Asaf Ali** | Hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank, 9 Aug 1942; underground leader |
| **Usha Mehta** | Ran the underground **Congress Radio**, Bombay |
| **Underground** | JP escaped **Hazaribagh** jail; Lohia, **Achyut Patwardhan**, Sucheta Kripalani, Biju Patnaik, R.P. Goenka |
| **Ballia** | Parallel govt, Aug 1942 — **Chittu Pandey** |
| **Tamluk** | **Jatiya Sarkar**, Midnapore, Dec 1942 – Sept 1944 |
| **Satara** | **Prati Sarkar**, 1943–45 — Y.B. Chavan, **Nana Patil**; longest-lived |
| **In detention** | Gandhi's fast of **21 days** (Feb 1943); **Kasturba** died there (Feb 1944); Gandhi released May 1944 |
| **Stayed away** | Muslim League, **Communist Party** ("people's war"), **Hindu Mahasabha**, princes |

**Don't confuse**
- **August Offer** = 1940 (Linlithgow); **August Kranti** = 8 August 1942 (Quit India); **Wavell Plan** = 1945.
- **Tamluk** (Bengal), **Ballia** (UP), **Satara** (Maharashtra, longest) — the three parallel governments.

**TL;DR**
- August Offer 8 Aug 1940; Lahore Resolution 23 Mar 1940 (Fazlul Haq).
- Individual Satyagraha from 17 Oct 1940: Vinoba, then Nehru.
- Cripps (Mar 1942): post-war Dominion, provinces may opt out — 'post-dated cheque'.
- Quit India: Wardha 14 Jul → Gowalia Tank 8 Aug 1942; parallel govts Ballia, Tamluk, Satara.
keyPoints: The August Offer was made on 8 August 1940.
Vinoba Bhave was the first individual satyagrahi (1940).
Gandhi called the Cripps offer 'a post-dated cheque'.
The Quit India resolution was passed at Gowalia Tank, Bombay.
Satara had the longest-lived parallel government of 1942–45.

items.title: The Road to 1947 — C.R. Formula to the Independence Act
items.body:
### The Road to 1947 — C.R. Formula to the Independence Act

**In one line**
From 1944 every attempt to keep India united failed on the Congress–League divide; the navy mutiny and Direct Action Day hastened the end.

**The story**
Released in 1944, Gandhi tried the **C.R. Formula** — a post-war **plebiscite** in Muslim areas — and talked to Jinnah in September 1944. **Wavell**'s **Simla Conference** (June–July 1945) broke down when the League claimed to name every Muslim member. The **Red Fort** trials of INA officers (November 1945) and the naval mutiny that began on **HMIS Talwar** on **18 February 1946** showed the army could no longer be trusted. Attlee sent the **Cabinet Mission** (**Pethick-Lawrence**, Cripps, **A.V. Alexander**); its plan of **16 May 1946** grouped provinces into **sections A, B and C**. Jinnah's **Direct Action Day** (16 August 1946) led to the Calcutta killings. Nehru's **Interim Government** took office on 2 September; the Constituent Assembly met on **9 December 1946**. Attlee set **June 1948** as the deadline, and Mountbatten's **3 June** Plan brought partition and freedom on **15 August 1947** under an Act passed on **18 July**.

#### 1944–1947

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **C.R. Formula** | 1944; League to back independence; post-war **plebiscite** in Muslim-majority areas; Jinnah rejected |
| **Gandhi–Jinnah talks** | **September 1944**, Bombay — failed |
| **Desai–Liaquat Pact** | Jan 1945; Bhulabhai **Desai** & **Liaquat** Ali Khan; Congress–League parity |
| **Wavell Plan / Simla Conference** | **Wavell**; Simla, 25 June–14 July 1945; failed — League claimed to nominate all Muslims |
| **INA trials** | **Red Fort**, **November 1945** (Shah Nawaz, Sahgal, Dhillon) |
| **RIN Mutiny** | **18 February 1946**, Bombay, on **HMIS Talwar**; spread to 78 ships (source PDF: 56); ended 23 Feb |
| **End of the mutiny** | **Patel and Jinnah** persuaded the ratings to **surrender**, 23 Feb 1946 |
| **Cabinet Mission** | Arrived 24 March 1946 (Attlee): **Pethick-Lawrence** (chair), Stafford Cripps, **A.V. Alexander** |
| **Plan** | **16 May 1946**: no Pakistan; union for defence, foreign affairs, communications; provinces grouped in **sections A, B and C**; constituent assembly |
| **Direct Action Day** | **16 August 1946**; Great Calcutta Killings; premier **Suhrawardy** |
| **Interim Government** | **2 September 1946**; Nehru Vice-President; League joined 26 Oct (**Liaquat** — Finance) |
| **Constituent Assembly** | First met **9 December 1946** (League boycotted) |
| **Attlee's statement** | **20 February 1947** — power to be transferred by **June 1948** |
| **Mountbatten Plan** | **3 June** 1947: partition; Punjab & Bengal assemblies vote; NWFP & Sylhet referendums; date advanced to **15 August 1947** |
| **Indian Independence Act** | Royal assent **18 July 1947**; **two dominions**; Viceroy's office ended; princes free |
| **Boundaries** | Sir Cyril **Radcliffe** — Punjab and Bengal boundary awards (17 Aug 1947) |
| **Governors-General** | Mountbatten first of free India; C. **Rajagopalachari** the **last** (only Indian); Jinnah for Pakistan |
| **Sapru Committee** | 1944–45 — constituent assembly, safeguards for minorities |

**Don't confuse**
- **Cripps Mission** (1942, Cripps alone) ≠ **Cabinet Mission** (1946, Cripps was one of three).
- **Wavell Plan** led to the **Simla Conference (1945)**; **Mountbatten Plan** = **3 June 1947**.

**TL;DR**
- C.R. Formula 1944; Gandhi–Jinnah talks Sept 1944; Desai–Liaquat Jan 1945; Simla Conference June 1945.
- INA trials Nov 1945; RIN Mutiny 18 Feb 1946 (HMIS Talwar).
- Cabinet Mission (Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, Alexander); plan 16 May 1946; Direct Action 16 Aug 1946.
- Interim Govt 2 Sept 1946; CA 9 Dec 1946; Attlee 20 Feb 1947; 3 June Plan; Act 18 July 1947.
keyPoints: The C.R. Formula (1944) proposed a post-war plebiscite.
The RIN Mutiny began on HMIS Talwar on 18 February 1946.
The Cabinet Mission Plan grouped provinces into sections A, B and C.
The Interim Government was formed on 2 September 1946.
The Indian Independence Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947.

items.title: Peasant Movements and Tribal Revolts — Full List
items.body:
### Peasant Movements and Tribal Revolts — Full List

**In one line**
Peasants fought planters, landlords and moneylenders; tribals fought outsiders who took their land and forests. The Congress drew many of these struggles into the national movement after 1917.

**The story**
Nineteenth-century peasants rose locally and were usually crushed, but each rising produced a law: the **Indigo Revolt** (1859–60, **Nadia**, celebrated in **Neel Darpan**) produced an Indigo Commission; the **Pabna** league led to the **Bengal Tenancy Act 1885**; the **Deccan Riots** (1875) to the **Relief Act of 1879**. In the twentieth century peasants joined national politics — **Baba Ramchandra**'s Awadh Kisan Sabha, **Madari Pasi**'s Eka, the Malabar **Moplahs**, Patel's **Bardoli** — and in **1936** the **All India Kisan Sabha** was formed with **Sahajanand Saraswati** and the Andhra leader **N.G. Ranga**. The last great struggles were **Tebhaga** (two-thirds), **Telangana** and **Punnapra–Vayalar**. Tribal revolts ran in parallel: the **Kol** (1831), the **Santhal** Hul of **Sidhu** and Kanhu (1855), **Birsa Munda**'s **Ulgulan** (1899–1900), and in Andhra's hills the **Khond** rising of **Chakra Bisoi** and the **Koya** revolts.

#### Peasant movements

| Movement | Place, leader and result |
|---|---|
| **Indigo Revolt** | 1859–60, Bengal; began in **Nadia** — Digambar & Bishnucharan **Biswas** |
| **Neel Darpan** | **Dinabandhu Mitra** (1860); English version published by Rev. **James Long** (fined, jailed) |
| **Indigo Commission** | **1860** (the source PDF prints 1869) |
| **Pabna** | 1873–76; Agrarian League; Ishan Chandra Roy, Shambhu Pal; → **Bengal Tenancy Act 1885** |
| **Deccan Riots** | **1875**, Poona & Ahmednagar (began at Supa); against moneylenders → **Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879** |
| **UP Kisan Sabha** | **1918** — Gauri Shankar Mishra, Indra Narayan Dwivedi; Malaviya's support |
| **Awadh Kisan Sabha** | 1920; **Baba Ramchandra** (Fiji-returned); Nehru helped |
| **Eka movement** | 1921–22, Hardoi–Bahraich; **Madari Pasi** |
| **Moplah rebellion** | 1921, Malabar; tenants vs landlords, turned communal; **Wagon Tragedy** (Nov 1921); Malabar Special Police |
| **Bardoli** | 1928, Patel; **22**% hike opposed; **Maxwell–Broomfield** inquiry reduced it to 6.03%; title "Sardar" |
| **Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha** | **1929**, Swami Sahajanand Saraswati |
| **All India Kisan Sabha** | Lucknow, **11 April 1936**; president **Sahajanand Saraswati**, secretary **N.G. Ranga**; Kisan Manifesto |
| **Tebhaga** | 1946–47, Bengal; sharecroppers (bargadars) to keep **two-thirds** |
| **Telangana struggle** | 1946–51; against deshmukhs, jagirdars, Razakars; abolished **vetti**; communist-led |
| **Punnapra–Vayalar** | 1946, **Travancore** — against Dewan C.P. Ramaswami Iyer |
| **Warli revolt** | 1945–46, Thane; **Godavari Parulekar** |

#### Tribal revolts

| Revolt | Place, leader and result |
|---|---|
| **Santhal Hul** | 1855–56, Rajmahal hills (Damin-i-koh); **Sidhu** & Kanhu; → **Santhal Parganas** district |
| **Kol rising** | 1831–32, Chotanagpur (Ranchi, Singhbhum); **Buddho Bhagat** |
| **Munda Ulgulan** | 1899–1900, Ranchi; **Birsa Munda** (died in jail June 1900); → **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908** |
| **Birsa Munda remembered** | **15 November** — **Janjatiya Gaurav Divas** (from 2021) |
| **Khond uprisings** | 1837–56, Odisha → Srikakulam/Visakhapatnam hills; **Chakra Bisoi**; against ban on meriah sacrifice, new taxes |
| **Koya revolts** | Eastern Godavari agency, 1803–1886; chiefs **Tomma** Dora (Sora); Rampa rising 1879–80; Raja Anantayyar 1886 |
| **Bhil revolts** | 1817–19, **Khandesh** (Western Ghats) |
| **Ramosi risings** | Western Ghats; Chittur Singh (1822), **Umaji Naik** |
| **Khasi rising** | 1829–33; **Tirot Singh**; against the Brahmaputra–Sylhet road |
| **Pahariya rising** | 1778, Rajmahal hills; land declared **damni-kol** |
| **Tana Bhagat** | 1914, Oraons of Chotanagpur; **Jatra Bhagat**; later Gandhian |
| **Zeliangrong / Heraka** | 1920s–30s, Manipur; **Jadonang** (hanged 1931), then Gaidinliu |
| **Bastar rebellion** | 1910; **Gunda Dhur** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Indigo Revolt (1859–60, Bengal)** ≠ **Champaran (1917, Bihar, tinkathia)** — both about indigo.
- **Kol** (Buddho Bhagat, 1831) ≠ **Munda** (Birsa, 1899) ≠ **Santhal** (Sidhu–Kanhu, 1855).
- The source PDF dates the Indigo Commission to 1869; the commission sat in **1860**.

**TL;DR**
- Indigo 1859–60 (Biswas brothers, Neel Darpan); Pabna → Tenancy Act 1885; Deccan Riots 1875 → Relief Act 1879.
- Awadh (Baba Ramchandra), Eka (Madari Pasi), Moplah 1921 (Wagon Tragedy), Bardoli 1928 (22%).
- AIKS 11 Apr 1936 Lucknow — Sahajanand, N.G. Ranga; Tebhaga 1946; Telangana 1946–51.
- Tribal: Kol 1831 (Buddho Bhagat), Santhal 1855 (Sidhu–Kanhu), Munda 1899 (Birsa), Khond (Chakra Bisoi), Koya (Tomma Dora).
keyPoints: Dinabandhu Mitra's Neel Darpan exposed the indigo planters.
The Deccan Riots led to the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879.
The All India Kisan Sabha (1936) had Sahajanand Saraswati as president and N.G. Ranga as secretary.
The Santhal rebellion (1855–56) was led by Sidhu and Kanhu.
Birsa Munda's Ulgulan led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908.

items.title: The Nationalist Press and the Press Laws
items.body:
### The Nationalist Press and the Press Laws

**In one line**
Newspapers carried nationalism to every town; the British answered with a series of press laws.

**The story**
Almost every nationalist leader ran a paper: **Naoroji** the Gujarati **Rast Goftar**, **Surendranath Banerjee** **The Bengalee**, the Ghosh brothers **Amrita Bazar Patrika** (which turned English overnight in 1878 to escape Lytton's Act), **G. Subramania Iyer** **The Hindu** and **Swadesamitran**, **Malaviya** **The Leader**, **Nehru** the **National Herald** (1938), Ambedkar **Bahishkrit Bharat**. Lytton's **Vernacular Press Act** (1878) was repealed by Ripon, but the Swadeshi years brought the **Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act** 1908 and the **Indian Press Act 1910**, which made presses deposit **securities**.

#### Papers and press laws

| Paper / law | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Amrita Bazar Patrika** | 1868, Jessore; **Sisir Kumar Ghosh** & Motilal Ghosh; turned English in 1878 to dodge the VPA |
| **The Hindu** | 1878, Madras — G. Subramania Iyer, Veeraraghavachariar; Iyer's Tamil **Swadesamitran** (1882) |
| **The Tribune** | 1881, Lahore — Dyal Singh **Majithia** |
| **The Bengalee** | 1862 (Girish Chandra Ghosh); S.N. Banerjee from 1879 |
| **Rast Goftar** | 1851, Gujarati — Dadabhai Naoroji |
| **The Leader** | Allahabad, 1909 — Madan Mohan **Malaviya** |
| **National Herald** | Lucknow, **1938** — Jawaharlal Nehru |
| **Hindustan Times** | Delhi, 1924; first editor K.M. **Panikkar** |
| **Bahishkrit Bharat** | 1927 — B.R. Ambedkar (Marathi) |
| **Bandi Jivan** | Sachindranath Sanyal |
| **Newspapers Act 1908** | Newspapers (**Incitement to Offences**) Act — seize presses |
| **Indian Press Act 1910** | Revived VPA-type powers; **securities** from presses |

**Don't confuse**
- **Kesari/Mahratta** = Tilak; **Bengalee** = S.N. Banerjee; **The Hindu** = G. Subramania Iyer; **Amrita Bazar Patrika** = Ghosh brothers.
- **Bande Mataram** was edited by Aurobindo (Calcutta) and also by Madame Cama (Paris) — two different papers.

**TL;DR**
- ABP 1868 (Ghosh brothers); The Hindu 1878 (G. Subramania Iyer); Tribune 1881 (Majithia).
- Leader (Malaviya); National Herald 1938 (Nehru); Bahishkrit Bharat (Ambedkar).
- Press laws: VPA 1878 → Newspapers Act 1908 → Indian Press Act 1910.
keyPoints: Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh.
G. Subramania Iyer started The Hindu and Swadesamitran.
Jawaharlal Nehru founded the National Herald in 1938.
The Indian Press Act 1910 revived the powers of the Vernacular Press Act.
Press laws: the Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908 allowed seizure of presses that printed incitement; the Indian Press Act 1910 demanded securities from presses.

items.title: For Mains — Freedom Movement & Revolutionaries
items.body:
### For Mains — the freedom movement as an analytical theme

**In one line**
For Mains you must argue, not list: show how the movement changed in method and base over time, and weigh the contribution of each stream.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC Paper-2 (Indian history and national movement) asks you to analyse phases, assess movements and compare streams — not merely recall dates.

**The dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Phases | Moderate (1885-1905) → Extremist/Swadeshi (1905-1917) → Gandhian mass phase (1919-1947) |
| Methods | Petitions → boycott/Swadeshi → non-violent mass satyagraha; parallel armed revolution |
| Social base | Elite professionals → urban middle class → peasants, women, students, workers |
| Streams | Congress constitutionalism · Gandhian mass politics · revolutionary nationalism · Bose/INA · peasant-tribal revolts |
| Significance | Built a nation-wide identity; forced constitutional advance; made the Raj ungovernable |
| Criticism/limits | Early mendicancy; Hindu-Muslim rift deepened by separate electorates; led to Partition |
| Way forward (legacy) | Secular, democratic, rights-based constitutionalism after 1947 |

**Data points / reports / judgments to quote**
- Naoroji's **Drain of Wealth** (*Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*, 1901) — the economic critique of empire.
- **Morley-Minto (1909)** separate electorates and the **Lucknow Pact (1916)** — the double-edged story of Hindu-Muslim politics.
- **Nehru Report (1928)** vs **Lahore Purna Swaraj (1929)** — the shift from Dominion Status to full independence.
- **Chauri Chaura (1922)** and the withdrawal of Non-Cooperation — Gandhi's non-negotiable non-violence.
- **INA Trials (1945-46)** and the **RIN Mutiny (1946)** — why the British finally decided to leave.

**The AP angle**
Andhra fed every phase: **Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion (1922-24)** linked tribal grievance to anti-colonial armed struggle, and Andhra's Non-Cooperation and no-tax campaigns show the national movement's regional depth.

**Use in answers**
- Example to cite: contrast the Moderates' 1892 Councils Act gain with the mass scale of Non-Cooperation to show the leap in method.
- A quote: Tilak's 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' to mark the Extremist turn.
- A diagram idea: a three-band timeline (Moderate · Extremist · Gandhian) with parallel 'revolutionary' and 'peasant-tribal' tracks running underneath.
keyPoints: Frame answers in three phases: Moderate (1885-1905), Extremist/Swadeshi (1905-1917), Gandhian mass phase (1919-1947).
Trace the shift in method (petition → boycott → mass satyagraha) and in social base (elite → peasants/women/workers).
Weigh four streams: Congress constitutionalism, Gandhian mass politics, revolutionary nationalism/INA, and peasant-tribal revolts.
Quote Drain of Wealth (1901), Lucknow Pact (1916), Nehru Report (1928) vs Purna Swaraj (1929), INA Trials/RIN Mutiny (1945-46).
